Implementing this algorithm on a 8-qubit superconducting quantum processor enabled us to accurately replicate a real-world dataset and outperform competing results for a specific binary classification task. Additionally, we applied this algorithm to a multi-state data task and achieved results on par with classical methods in a more efficient manner.

Previous studies have demonstrated that changing the fundamental frequency (F0) is the most effective way to control pitch in speech, yet many neural speech synthesis systems struggle to do so without compromising their synthesis quality. A recent system called FastPitch uses neurostyle control to enable F0 control, but even FastPitch often fails to produce high-quality speech when the speaker's F0 range is significantly different from the target F0. To improve pitch controllability in FastPitch, this study introduces a pitch augmentation method. By training FastPitch with artificially created speech recordings that include the speaker's F0 deviations alongside their natural speech, this method enhances the system's ability to change its pitch without affecting its ability to preserve its natural speech characteristics. As a result, this study's experiments indicate that the pitch augmentation condition yields a mean opinion score (MOS) of 4.42, a significant improvement over FastPitch's 3.95, with only a slight decrease in its high-quality speech rate (about 1%), showcasing the method's effectiveness.

This research targets the problem of extracting semantic information from satellite images by employing satellite passes for feature extraction and spatiotemporal reasoning. Satellite data is characterized by extensive data sequences, intricate structures, long-term dependencies, and variable-length temporal intervals. To tackle these challenges, we introduce a novel transformer-based model, called Hopper, which is designed to capture multi-hop relationships between satellite appearances. This model employs a multi-stage architecture to aggregate and integrate information from different passes, accounting for varying time intervals, long-term temporal dependencies, and multi-hop interactions. To evaluate its effectiveness, we have developed a large, manually-annotated dataset and conducted experiments on both manual and automated datasets, demonstrating the superiority of Hopper over baseline models.

This paper presents theoretical findings on the production of same-flavor opposite-sign charged leptons paired with $b\bar{b}$ quarks using the narrow-width approximation for the $W$ boson, valid at leading order in QCD. We derive the virtual correction for this process via the $W$ boson's loop insertion and confirm that the results match those from the $W$+3 jets process calculated at leading order. Additionally, we investigate how the results for $q\bar{q} \to \ell^+ \ell^- \ell^+ \ell^-$ contribute to the $W$ mass reconstruction.

To evaluate the effectiveness of a telepresence robot (TR) communication system, which prioritizes user experience over system performance, traditional performance metrics are insufficient. A new, interactive quality-of-experience assessment method has been developed, incorporating remote control of the TR to simulate real-world interactions. The proposed approach, involving a multi-dimensional rating scale, interactive voice response, and 3D motion simulation, was tested with untrained users who provided quality-of-experience scores while navigating the TR. The results showed that the proposed approach yielded more realistic QoE evaluations than traditional methods and that the current TR technology falls short in meeting user expectations for seamless interactions.

The increasing accessibility of Bayesian statistics has led to a surge in adoption across multiple social sciences. This surge is largely attributed to the versatility of mixed models, which have long been staples in large-scale data analysis. This paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of Bayesian hierarchical linear models, exploring their relevance in various research contexts and highlighting the benefits of using Bayesian methods. A hands-on approach will be taken, with code and practical examples, to facilitate replication and reference.

The model's initial state is defined by the number of players (N) held in captivity, with half being Mafias and the other players not. A player's faction is unknown to other players. Each round consists of two phases: first, players take individual actions to either suspect or not suspect another player, followed by a public revelation of Mafias based on suspicions. In the second phase, Mafias eliminate non-Mafias, with both Mafias and non-Mafias Mafias (elimination is implied for) surviving. A win condition is established for Mafias if there are at least one Mafias left alive and a loss if there are none. Outside of these win/loss conditions, Mafias can win through time. A player can communicate through the game only through their actions, with no direct communication possible. A numerical model of the game's dynamics is developed, with an analytical expression derived for the win/loss ratio as a function of time and players. A detailed description of the numerical method used to solve the model is provided, with the corresponding code available online.

This research investigates how two massive planets form at a time when a substantial amount of gas is still present in the disk. As a result, the planets experience gas accumulation, which affects their mass and the evolution of the surrounding disk. A series of interactive numerical simulations revealed that concurrent planet formation is marked by mutual influence and a complex gas dynamics. While the disk's gas distribution impacts the planets' orbital paths and mass growth, the planets' growth also shape the disk's gas configuration. A simplified model was then developed to understand the evolution of the planets' masses and the disk's eccentricity. This led to three possible outcomes for the planets' final configurations: (i) both planets becoming massive gas giants due to concurrent gas accumulation, (ii) the development of an outer hole in the disk as one planet migrates, with the other remaining in an inner orbit, or (iii) the planets becoming massive solids due to reduced gas availability in the disk.

The ability to conduct heat and charge across different materials is fundamental to the operation of various devices and systems, and is particularly relevant in one-dimensional nanomaterials. We have investigated the heat transfer mechanisms between and within carbon nanotubes using an Inca model and Raman spectroscopy, and found evidence that phonons facilitate electronic transport between tubes. This suggests that the heat and charge transport properties of the film are interconnected. We have also shown that the heat transfer between tubes is supported by an extended network of low-frequency vibrations, and that the heat transfer rate is determined by the temperature difference and the characteristics of the individual nanotubes. These findings provide new insights into the heat and charge transport mechanisms in carbon nanotube films, and highlight the importance of considering the interactions between and within one-dimensional systems of nanomaterials.

In high-dimensional data sets, the entropy of neighboring points increases due to randomness, which can be leveraged for clustering purposes. Therefore, a novel entropy-based approach for clustering in high-dimensional data sets is introduced. This method adapts the traditional fuzzy k-means clustering technique by modifying the objective function with an entropy component and adjusting cluster radius limits automatically. As a result, the need for manual pre-processing to reduce dimensionality in advance of clustering can be bypassed. The effectiveness of this method was tested using simulated data and real-world examples, which demonstrated its superiority over the original entropy-based adaptive fuzzy k-means approach in terms of accuracy and robustness.

The Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) algorithm has been highly sought after for nearly a decade due to its potential to build highly scalable neural networks. Unfortunately, its training process is plagued by a 'deadlock' that causes poor convergence and slow learning, rendering it nearly unusable. In this study, we not only uncover the root cause of the 'deadlock' but also develop two innovative algorithms to overcome it. Our solutions, 'Dynamic Channel Assignment' and'sparse assignment with an additional memory layer', have been proven to yield comparable results to the current state-of-the-art method while allowing for significant reductions in both computational requirements and memory usage.

This research explores token-firing circuits, mathematical representations of both genus 0 automata and genus g Jacobians' theta functions, with a special focus on genus 1 and 2 circuits and their relation to theta functions and Prym varieties. Genus g circuits are shown to represent a special class of forms on the genus g Jacobian, with specific relationships in the cases of genus 1 and 2. In response to questions raised by D. Gottesman, this research demonstrates that any token-firing circuit with a rank greater than its output dimension can be transformed into a simplified circuit with a rank equal to its output dimension, with a corresponding flow on the line.

A theoretical model suggests that quantum gravity may impose a global symmetry constraint on the cosmological field, limiting the average change in the Wilson coefficient of electromagnetic birefringence. We evaluate two cosmological birefringence tests - the QCD axion and the plasma - to estimate the expected change in $a_1$ and $a_2$ coefficients in the Standard Model Extension. We then apply these findings to a fundamental quantum gravity theory, such as the CHL 6-point gauge theory, to set a lower bound on the global symmetry disruption. We discover that our birefringence bounds significantly outperform the cosmic bounds, and are also more stringent than the matrix element bounds. We further analyze how our birefringence bounds compare to the cosmic bounds and discuss their implications.

Our research presents new far-UV observations of a luminous star in the globular cluster NGC 4147, obtained with the UVIT instrument on the AstroSat satellite. These findings are combined with existing HST and UVIT near-UV data to determine the multi-colour optical and near-UV magnitudes of the brightest cluster stars. Using two-colour diagrams, we identified and differentiated different evolutionary stages of these stars, specifically white dwarfs, horizontal branch stars, and asymptotic giant branch stars. Furthermore, by cross-referencing our data with HST images, we refined the optical and near-UV magnitudes of these stars, specifically two HB stars and an AGB star, enabling us to assess the cluster's HB morphology. Our analysis suggests a bimodal HB distribution, featuring a UV-bright blue HB sub-population, likely the result of the cluster's metal 3 and [Fe/H] 0.8 characteristics.

We introduce a theorem which states that for flows with transferable action on a compact $n$-dimensional smooth manifold, the action's isotopy height is capped at $n+1$. This theorem falls under the category of b-principles which govern situations where a topological property is restricted to become a homotopy invariant. Our proof relies on an application of the transfer technique combined with the works of Fabes, Murty, Palka, Sarnak, and Swinnerton-Dyer on the algebraic Kummer surface's finiteness theorem as well as an application of the geometric analysis of the moduli space of bundles on the Kummer surface proposed by Hirzebruch-Mumford.

Deep learning networks' transferability has long been a topic of discussion. Researchers initially focused on understanding how previous experience influences future learning, but later explored the connection between local generalization and transferability. This paper argues that two widely accepted assumptions about transferability are flawed. Firstly, simply aligning data distributions does not guarantee improved performance. Secondly, there is no direct correlation between local hyperparameter optimization and transferability. Our findings are substantiated by experiments and theoretical proofs. We further provide insights into why hyperparameter optimization often appears to facilitate transferability, and suggest potential future research directions.

In various scenarios, such as mobilizing crowds or promoting vaccines, it is crucial to effectively disseminate information to a maximum number of people as quickly as possible. Researchers have studied the average time it takes for a message to reach a significant portion of a network in various scenarios. These studies were conducted on both real-world and artificially created networks of individuals. When examining networks of a type known as scale-free networks, a differing trend was observed. Specifically, networks composed of many interconnected clusters of nodes, which are characterized by a high value of a particular mathematical ratio, display a more efficient spread of the message. This efficiency is attributed to the organization of the nodes within separate clusters, which enhances global communication.

We establish a precise measurement of "distinctiveness" for families of Lagrangian homotopy equivalences by extending Thomas-Yau's concept and making it applicable to Lagrangian Floer theory. This involves modifying the Lagrangian Floer theory to incorporate a weight function, which can take values of 0 or 1, to reflect the theory's distinctiveness. As an application, we demonstrate the distinctiveness of Lagrangian branes under various conditions, such as minimal conditions, incompressibility, free loop negativity, and homotopy equivalences' characteristics.

A precise analysis of a single-mode fiber link has been developed using the time-domain standard perturbation model. This model provides an exact discrete-time equation, revealing that previously underestimated effects such as four-photon and five-photon interactions are actually negligible. However, in contrast, effects involving three photons and damping are non-negligible. It is discovered that the standard perturbation approach fails to yield an accurate solution due to an infinite sum of non-negligible terms. A novel method is proposed to solve the exact discrete-time equation and the equation for power, and these methods are then used to develop corrected equations for the standard perturbation approach. As a result, a modified version of the standard perturbation approach is possible, which offers a flexible way to incorporate certain nonlinear effects into the equation for power and the probability of photon piracy.

Future mobile phones are expected to serve as sensors and interfaces for a global population, fulfilling essential health and environmental needs, as well as providing entertainment options. This document provides an overview of digital evasion assaults occurring on Android operating systems. Evading digital countermeasures is an essential aspect of warfare, cyber warfare, and intelligence gathering. This study offers a comprehensive summary of evasion assaults on Android devices, covering the history of these attacks, notable instances, and evasion countermeasures.

This paper introduces Ozy, a versatile cluster cluster manager, which provides a unified framework for scheduling and managing complex parallel computations across diverse hardware platforms. Ozy is particularly well-suited for executing high-performance parallel tasks on specialized hardware, such as GPUs, KNLs, and ASICs. Its key features include a centralized system for managing parallel tasks, a dynamic scheduler, a modular plugin architecture, and a real-time system monitoring tool. Ozy's design is characterized by a minimal set of built-in capabilities, instead focusing on providing users with freedom to choose and integrate custom plugins tailored to their specific needs. Ozy's architecture is comprised of three primary layers: the cluster vessel, representing the cluster hardware infrastructure; the orchestration vessel, responsible for scheduling and job management; and the application vessel, encompassing the parallel applications themselves. Ozy's design enables users to integrate custom plugins to address a wide range of challenges, from hardware management to application-level optimization.

Quantum Hall phases exhibit remarkable characteristics, including intense magnetic fields and closely packed charge distributions. Landau-level repulsion undermines the principle of two distinct phases - 5/3 and 5/2, resulting in an unusual phase emergence from this conflict. Utilizing exact-exponential-U methods, our research has found this reentrant phase, influenced by moderate Landau-level interactions. We have also discovered that this reentrant phase transitions occur at finite coupling strengths and exhibit energy per particle minima. Our results demonstrate that in the presence of Landau-level repulsion, this reentrant phase can exist, contrasting with the phase diagrams produced by the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model.

Our analysis contradicts a recent research claim that cosmological black holes are described by the Thakurta metric. In fact, the Thakurta metric has a mass function that decreases with mass and redshift, and this issue cannot be resolved by adjusting coupling constants. Additionally, the presence of a bare cosmological constant in the Hamiltonian also poses a problem. The LIGO-Virgo collaboration's data on binary black hole mergers provides a means to determine the mass density of primordial black holes, and our results show that their constraints on $\Gamma-\gamma$ remain unchanged.

The formation of planets through pebble accumulation is studied in a 400 solar mass protostellar disk with varying levels of density, spanning from 1.0 to 3.0 grams per cubic centimeter. Simulations reveal that a disk's density affects the planets formed, with a 200 Earth mass super-Earth or mini-Neptune typically emerging in a disk with a density of 2.0 grams per cubic centimeter. A denser disk produces heavier planets, while a less dense disk produces smaller, less massive planets. To achieve consistency with observed planet mass distributions, our findings suggest that density fluctuations in protostellar disks could account for the diversity of planet masses. Specifically, our model indicates that 70% of super-Earths and 30% of mini-Neptunes have masses below 2.0 M_Earth, with 70% of super-Earths and mini-Neptunes existing in regions with densities above 2.0 g/cm^3 and 1.0 g/cm^c, respectively.

We examine how overparameterization in deep neural networks can lead to accurate generalization, not despite computational limitations, but actually due to them. Our study suggests that overparameterization in non-linear models with limited computational resources leads to smaller generalization errors and more predictable results compared to models with infinite computational capacity. This is because overparameterization in models with limited computational resources reduces the likelihood of overfitting by spreading data errors across different subspaces, whereas overparameterization in models with infinite computational resources can only delay overfitting, ultimately resulting in same-level generalization errors. This unique finding relies on our analysis of the generalization errors in linear and non-linear neural networks with varying degrees of computational resources, from the perspective of the Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory.

For every numerable abelian group, denoted $\Gamma$, consisting of elements with summations that produce a dense set of real numbers when combined, we demonstrate the existence of specific "Bohr structures". These structures are characterized by a set of finitely many elements whose sum and inverse sum can generate a dense set of $\Gamma$, thus providing a generalized version of the "Bohr structure" theorem originally applied to the integers. Additionally, we prove the density of the set resulting from taking all possible measures on the group $\Gamma$ with Dirac masses at points that are linear combinations of its elements, thus extending a previous result by Bergelson, Furstenberg, and Host.

The Dial-a-Ride Problem's metropolitan variant is particularly demanding due to an exceptionally large solution search space, thereby making trial-and-error solutions highly impractical. Researchers have proposed reduced-cost exact methods, such as Contraction and Synchronization, which rapidly produce high-quality lower and upper bounds, but only infrequently converge to optimal solutions. We introduce the Branch and Trim method, an enhanced variant of this approach, aimed at increasing the frequency of optimal solution discovery. We describe the algorithm's key components, including reduced-cost set partitioning and optimization, trimmed search spaces, and branching. We also outline additional techniques to accelerate convergence, such as parallel processing, and demonstrate its effectiveness in a comprehensive computational experiment.

In e-commerce, visual information is crucial for classifying products and determining descriptions, with human recognition abilities influenced by past experiences and cultural background. To mimic this, we've developed an e-commerce recognition multi-modal pretraining (ERMPT) framework that incorporates recognition capabilities into computer vision. By utilizing large-scale real-world data and incorporating knowledge of object categories from industry knowledge bases, ERMPT fine-tunes visual representations to match human understanding. Specifically, it uses a cultural-dependent bias loss to align human and computer object representations, with results showing ERMPT outperforms current top models in multiple e-commerce tasks and improves product classification accuracy by 11% from random initialization.

Recent breakthroughs in brain imaging technologies have made it possible to obtain detailed insights into elderly brains, enabling the identification of early-stage Alzheimer's disease. By leveraging sophisticated analysis methods, 3D brain maps can be generated, revealing subtle alterations caused by the disease. Statistical models can then use these maps to forecast whether Alzheimer's will eventually occur and predict when this will happen. Our research introduces a novel framework that employs Deep InfoMax to enhance the brain mapping process, yielding better insights and more accurate predictions. By fine-tuning Deep InfoMax with a large dataset, we achieved remarkable results, outperforming existing methods. Our findings indicate that this method can accurately predict Alzheimer's based on early-stage imaging data and identify key features associated with the disease.

We present a groundbreaking innovation in natural language processing utilizing a novel type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) that seamlessly integrates with human cognition. Our interaction-driven RNN model effectively merges top-down and bottom-up information streams, mirroring the complex process of human language semantics comprehension. We thoroughly test the model's capabilities on various benchmark tasks, including the ReClor dataset for Common Ground Estimation and the Winograd Semantic Parsing Evaluation Corpus. Our comparative analysis with leading state-of-the-art RNN-based models demonstrates the superior performance of our proposed model.

In systems with strong spin-orbit interaction, interest centers on whether accurate modeling can be achieved through perturbative methods. For systems like heavy disordered metals where spin-orbit interaction is relatively weak, this question takes on a different form. In such cases, other effects like electron-electron interactions and long-range Coulomb forces are significant. In a recent study, researchers used numerical methods to explore the impact of electron-electron interactions on spin-orbit behavior in a two-dimensional metal. They discovered that in the strong interaction regime, the spin-orbit behavior is enhanced, resulting in a larger effective spin-orbit coupling constant. This outcome has important implications for understanding magnetic properties, the emergence of topological phases, and other phenomena in these systems, which may be realized in an experimental model like a graphene system with high doping levels.

In this paper, we explore an innovative approach to the cosmic censorship conjecture known as the Metastable Conformal Shadow Universe (MCSU). It proposes that a certain type of spacetime singularity can form when a black hole's shadow transitions from one conformal frame to another, potentially preventing the full transition if the timescale for the transition is longer than that for evaporation to occur. The MCSU theorem has the following implications: (1) it significantly broadens the scope of the cosmic censorship conjecture, (which it may or may not satisfy), (2) it offers a new perspective on the stability of black holes that is consistent with the concept of a shadow, and (3) it provides a new understanding of the concept of black hole stability that is distinct from the mathematical model of black hole stability. The theoretical framework of the MCSU is rooted in a specific model of spherically symmetric black holes, but it can be generalized to other types of black holes. The paper also discusses the generalization of the concept to scenarios where spacetime is not spherically symmetric.

The effectiveness of artificial intelligence (AI) medical instruments, such as those used for diagnosis and prognosis, is typically evaluated based on their performance using training data. Yet, to be truly useful, these tools must also operate accurately in unforeseen environments. Unfortunately, determining their performance in such scenarios proves difficult due to the lack of relevant data. In this context, assessing medical instruments in unknown environments poses a particularly difficult challenge due to the inherent risks and potential consequences of inaccurate diagnoses or prognoses. Our proposed solution involves using conformal forecasting tests to evaluate AI medical instruments in unfamiliar settings by comparing their performance with established standards, set by the instruments themselves, under two types of distribution shifts - horizontal and vertical. Our approach encompasses multiple testing scenarios, including when only the data is altered, when the underlying condition changes, and when both the data and the underlying condition change. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of this approach in gauging AI medical instruments in unfamiliar environments, as well as their general applicability to any scenario involving distribution shifts.

In solution, DNA exists in a dynamic state with the presence of counterions and water molecules which influence electrostatic properties at the local level, leading to a DNA conformation that appears more flexible than in an aqueous environment with ion presence, yet less flexible than in a pure aqueous environment with neutralized ions. A recent study has demonstrated that a specific simulation method that adjusts base stiffness in line with DNA's local electrostatic properties achieves a better fit with NMR data compared to other methods, such as the widely used Parm90 parameter set. Additionally, the stiffness-based method has shown improved agreement with the average radius of gyre (Rg) values obtained from small-angle neutron scattering data for double and single-stranded DNA.

The Advanced Encryption Standard uses various algorithms to perform entropy compression and diffusion across its S-Box components. This paper focuses on evaluating the effectiveness of the ANS method in achieving both goals. In terms of diffusion, the paper introduces a new criterion to check if the ANS box exhibits hyperbolic behavior, and demonstrates that only with certain conditions can this occur. Consequently, the proof of diffusion effectiveness is based on transforming the S-Box into a Markov matrix with positive eigenvalues, and shows that hyperbolicity is essential for this purpose. In relation to compression, the paper examines the multi-dimensional distribution of ANS output points and shows that, under specific conditions, these points form the vertices of a central hypercube. Based on this, the paper proves that the ANS S-Box is capable of performing non-trivial compression, and provides conditions under which it can achieve ideal compression.

Pore fluids in cement-based materials are dynamic, with the cement paste and admixtures constantly interacting. Admixtures, specifically foaming agents and air-entraining agents, alter the fluid's properties in response to changes in the environment. This paper examines how the presence of these admixtures impacts the dielectric behavior of the pore fluid, with the ultimate goal of developing models that accurately describe the dielectric properties of cement-based materials over a broad frequency spectrum.

To investigate heavy-heavy clusters in baryon and meson octets, a simple, potential model is applied, using constituent quarks. The model's parameters are determined through a least squares fit to the masses of various hadrons, with the exception of $X(3872)$, which is included due to its intriguing nature. The model then predicts masses for the remaining unknown octostructures. The predictions for the $D^{\ast} D^{\ast}$
and $\bar D^{\ast} D^{\ast}$ clusters differ from previous models, notably those utilizing chiral dynamics or relativistic quark models. The model's results for the $DD^{\ast}$ cluster also diverge from a 2016 prediction using a chiral approach. The model's outcomes for the $BB$ cluster match a 2013 prediction using relativistic quark models. The model's results for the $DD^{\ast}\bar D^{\ast}$ and $\bar D^{\ast}\bar D^{\ast}D^{\ast}$ clusters appear unstable. The model's predictions for the $X(3872)$ assume it contains $D^0D^{\ast 0}$ or $\bar D^0\bar D^{*0}$, yielding mass values of 3.11 or 3.09 GeV, respectively. The model's predictions for the $X(3930)$ assume a $D^{\ast}\bar D

The use of micro unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in a military context is becoming increasingly significant. These small drones are easy to acquire, allowing private entities and governments to possess them. As a result, there is a growing need for armed forces and security organizations to assess the capabilities of these UAVs, which they may encounter in a variety of settings, including online sources. The time-consuming nature of manually analyzing individual systems to understand their capabilities is a major obstacle. Our research aims to develop a solution by leveraging natural language processing to identify key performance indicators of military UAVs in online publications and databases, using a systematic approach to establish a standardized reference. The established reference will serve as a foundation for creating an automatic analysis tool that can quickly assess unfamiliar UAVs based on official evaluations and comparison with established best practices.

The information contained in the three-dimensional structure of Lyman-$\alpha$ forest flux fluctuations at small scales is difficult to analyze directly because it is heavily affected by non-linear effects and intra-halo pressure. However, a new method has been developed to extract baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) features and a Hubble rate estimate from these fluctuations by utilizing a Gaussian process to filter the data and a BAO model based on a two-point correlation function template. This method is highly effective, yielding a combined value of $H=67.66\pm0.23$ km/s/Mpc and $d_z=4.743\pm0.0006$ at $z=2.40$ from a simulated Lyman-$\alpha$ flux through a Gaussian process. Furthermore, the simulated Lyman-$\alpha$ flux exhibits a BAO signal-to-noise ratio of 2.67 and a precision of $0.53\%$, and it is expected that with larger datasets, BAO features and the Hubble constant can be determined with $1\%$ precision even at higher redshifts. This method is highly promising for future large-scale Lyman-$\alpha$ flux datasets to achieve $1\%$ precision at $z>2$ and to combine with other cosmological constraints to achieve $0.5\%$ precision independently.

Researchers at the Fermilab proton upgrade have achieved an innovative breakthrough 
in emittance exchange technology. A specially designed beamline allowed for the 
spatial separation of transverse and longitudinal beam components, followed by a 
targeted manipulation of the beams to recreate the original beam pattern. This 
groundbreaking experiment confirmed that a full emittance transfer is attainable 
and also allowed for the demonstration of a novel scheme for emittance boosting, 
which may be crucial for future high-intensity proton upgrade projects at Fermilab.

This study explores the challenge of predicting and forecasting future driving behaviors, and how past actions can inform future decisions, particularly with regards to lane changes. A critical finding is that predicting lane changes from past data alone is insufficient, as it often results in inaccurate predictions due to random events and inconsistencies. To address this issue, a novel forecasting model has been developed which incorporates random events, lane change history, and probability calculations to accurately predict lane changes. This involves leveraging conditional variational autoencoders and a socially-aware approach to reevaluate predictions, especially useful in dense traffic scenarios. A comprehensive evaluation has been conducted on the Interaction dataset, and the results demonstrate the model's accuracy and social intelligence.

Boltzmann machines, an fundamental model in statistical deep learning, have been examined to contrast information-theoretic metrics of complexity. While some of these metrics appear consistent in their assessment, others reveal discordance, which may be attributed to distinct modes of assessment (macro or micro) as well as variations in the type of information considered (direct observations vs. inferred knowledge of probability distributions). By employing metrics such as mutual information, Bayesian entropy, Markov entropy, and effective channel capacity, the complexities of Boltzmann machines, characterized by interacting spin variables, could be distinguished based on their visible or hidden components. Specifically, higher mutual information and Markov entropy were found to correlate with higher Bayesian and effective channel capacities, indicating that macro-level information-theoretic metrics of complexity may be aligned across visible and hidden layers of the model.

Swarm robotics benefits from interactions with humans, including instruction via hand gestures. Research has focused on recognizing hand gestures to enable swarm robots to interpret commands from their human counterparts. Previous studies have concentrated on collecting and analyzing data, overlooking the distribution of commands among individuals. This work introduces a decentralized system allowing each robot to verify the identity of a commanding human through sequential hand motion analysis, enacted via the robots' local observations. This approach supports recognition among multiple humans issuing distinct commands to different swarms.

In medical diagnostics, especially for blood-related conditions, accurate analysis of blood cell types is vital. This process can be streamlined and improved by employing a combination of advanced neural networks, which utilize data from a widely available image database, the DTU Image Database, to learn and categorize blood cell types. By merging models from the Specialized and Generalized approaches, we achieve enhanced performance and a higher degree of confidence in our blood cell categorization. This combination not only minimizes errors but also allows for the introduction of a new performance metric, F1-score, which provides a more nuanced understanding of performance, especially for rare cell types.

Our research delves into the assembly of the Hubbard model's ground state via the variational method. We've discovered a method to determine the optimal variational parameters, enabling the system to bypass excited states and directly reach the ground state. We've also found a way to achieve this change rapidly by adjusting a small number of variational parameters. We've demonstrated that this approach can be realized experimentally by performing quantum gas experiments and shown that it's feasible to implement in ultracold two-dimensional Hubbard systems.

A new technique for modeling the high-velocity decoloration of supersonic exhausts is developed using an empirical approach from a digital painting method, specifically 'hue shifting.' This technique is designed for supersonic exhausts that change color as they interact with their surroundings, particularly in the case of blue flame burning in a supersonic atmosphere. It is based on the idea that different colors in an image can move independently of each other, which is similar to how different frequencies can change independently in a given space. It is notable that this technique does not rely on the use of artificial colors or data from chemical reactions, but rather relies on natural color transitions within a given environment. It is also capable of handling complex interactions between objects and color spaces, which is evident in scenarios such as jet interactions with atmospheric layers and atmospheric variations in scenarios such as jet interactions with atmosphere and atmospheric variations.

The Taylor series for the exponential function e^x, with x being a variable, does not necessarily converge for all values of x beyond a certain point. This fact highlights the need to develop an alternative, exponential series-like approximation for e^x, valid for larger values of x. Such an approximation would have the form e^x = a_0 + (x-1)(e_1 + x(e_2 + x(e_3 +...)). This paper derives the coefficients (e_n)_(n=1) infinity in a straightforward manner and shows that they equal the zeros of the function e^-xU'(x), where U(x) is the utility function, which increases for larger values of x. This property allows us to establish that the coefficients (e_n)_(n=1) infinity are positive and asymptotically behave like e^(e_n)_(n=1)_(L) with e_1 > 1, e_n > e_n-1, and e_L being the last one, as n approaches infinity, where n approaches infinity, a limit denoted by L, which is the point where the convergence of the Taylor series stops, a L > 1. This property allows us to establish that the coefficients (e_n)_(n=1) infinity are positive and asymptotically behave like e^(e_n)_(n=1)_(L) with e_1 > 1, e_n > e_n-

Given a surface with negative curvature and a removed region bounded by $N$ closed curves, where each boundary component has a branch number of $2n$ or less, we demonstrate that there is a harmonic function on the removed region that can be extended harmonically to the entire surface, and its gradient at every point is non-zero.  Additionally, this extension can be achieved in a manner that is continuous and differentiable outside of the removed region, and its gradient at every point is non-zero.  This result has far-reaching implications, particularly in the area of mapping degree.  As a consequence of this result, we prove that any surface with a non-negative curvature that contains a removed region bounded by a single simple closed curve can be uniformlyized using a harmonic function, and its gradient at every point is non-zero.  Furthermore, we utilize this result to simplify and modify multiple existing theorems and concepts in the field, and we present several new applications and generalizations, including a new approach to the Riemann Mapping Theorem.

A novel concept for generating, fine-tuning, and manipulating ultra-high-field laser-plasma sources is developed, enabling the production of tunable x-ray and soft gamma-ray radiation. This is achieved through a combination of laser and plasma wave interactions, where the inherent plasma waves are modulated by a co-propagating laser, enabling the adjustment of radiation groups based on desired applications. To further enhance its capabilities, the source can be combined with an external magnetic field, giving rise to a synchotron-like radiation effect. As a result, the proposed source may produce a broader spectrum ranging from the infrared to soft gamma rays. To demonstrate its potential, the idea involves creating a pair of x-ray and keV gamma-ray sources separated by a narrow energy gap, where the sources can be utilized for studying quantum electrodynamics, testing vacuum energy and the photon-photon interaction, and exploring high-field strong-laser interactions in plasmas.

A critical parameter, $m_{12}$, in two-Higgs-doublet models, determines the mass gap between the neutral scalar fields after electroweak symmetry breaking. We examine how this gap influences the responses of various physical observables to high-energy collisions. Our findings indicate that this is a responsive parameter, as visible in the differences between the production amplitudes before and after the symmetry breaking. However, precise measurements of these responses are hampered by significant uncertainties, primarily due to limitations in our understanding of the strong interaction.

The RDF data format is beneficial for web data, allowing information to be easily accessed and linked. However, existing data on the web is often represented in other formats, such as XML with constraints defined by XSDs and Shape Maps. These constraints ensure data accuracy by validating individual data sets. To leverage the benefits of RDF, data can be converted from other formats, but current conversion processes overlook the validation aspect, making the resulting data susceptible to errors. To address this, a solution is proposed to transfer data from various formats, including one based on XML with XSDs and Shape Maps, onto an RDF data format that incorporates XSDs and Shape Maps, thereby enabling data validation as it is converted.

A multivariate boundary estimation method, known as StoNED, uses non-parametric convex regression to analyze data from diverse sources. This technique has been employed in numerous studies to understand the nature of data boundaries. In this research, we present pyStoNED, a Python library that offers a simple and effective implementation of StoNED. Through a series of practical applications, we demonstrate the effectiveness of StoNED using pyStoNED, comparing it to alternative techniques. Furthermore, we expand on StoNED by developing two new variants that improve its performance in real-world scenarios. The pyStoNED library and enhanced methods are now available to support reproducible research and method comparisons in fields such as computer science, statistics, and data science.

In the standard model, the Higgs boson is a crucial component that gives mass to fundamental particles, and its discovery was a significant breakthrough in physics in 2012. Due to the Higgs' inherent connection to new physics beyond the standard model, it is a prime focus of further investigation. One of the most promising approaches to probing this link involves examining the Higgs' properties, such as its production characteristics. Light Higgs regions, where the Higgs is less massive than the top quark, are particularly intriguing in this regard, as they are aligned with specific theories of new physics. However, in these areas, searches for the Higgs are complicated by the presence of top quarks and associated radiation. To address this, a study is presented that focuses on detecting the Higgs in the top-antitop Higgs (t tbar h) production mode at the LHC using advanced techniques. By combining data from the LHC's run 1 and run 2, and employing the latest version of the CMS software, it is possible to achieve a level of sensitivity to the Higgs that is comparable to the latest dedicated searches.

Pretrained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated impressive cross-domain and cross-task generalization capabilities. Recent studies have explored the potential of PLMs in leveraging in-domain data for improved out-of-domain task performance. Analyzing PLMs' internal representations can provide valuable insights into their generalization behavior, while also enabling applications such as unsupervised and few-shot learning. However, existing methods primarily rely on shallow features like word embeddings, neglecting deeper representations and resulting in limited improvements for tasks like unsupervised and few-shot learning. To address this, we investigate the use of PLMs' high-level semantic representations, specifically contextualized embeddings, to improve task performance. Our work involves developing a novel method utilizing contextualized embeddings in an unsupervised setting, as well as a novel few-shot learning framework based on self-supervised pretraining. Our experiments with the GLUE benchmark reveal that contextualized embeddings yield significant improvements over word embeddings, leading to 8.6% higher F1 score on average. Moreover, our proposed few-shot learning method achieves an impressive 20.1% relative improvement over the Fast Adapt framework. Our results also demonstrate the efficacy of contextualized embeddings in enhancing PLMs' generalization capabilities, and highlight their potential in unlocking the full potential of PLMs in unsupervised and few-shot learning applications.

The accuracy of speech-based applications heavily relies on high-quality speech recognition, a complex task for limited domains like open-source software development. We present a freely accessible, web-based tool that automates speech-to-text transcription for German CS:GO live broadcasts, utilizing a custom-trained neural network model. Our work combines elements from two established frameworks, ResNet and CNN-LSTM, to create an effective end-to-end model. We also explore the impact of preprocessing techniques, specifically log-mel spectrogram normalization, on the model's performance. To enhance the model's domain-specific understanding, we incorporate a vocabulary filter that replaces irrelevant terms with 'unknown', ensuring precise representations of domain-specific content. We evaluate the efficacy of this approach on a dataset of 1,804 hours, achieving a word error rate of 64.6% and improving upon a leading open-source model by 8.4%.

The origin of Be-type stars is still unclear, specifically regarding how they transform from B-type stars into Be-type stars, which is the focus of this study. To better understand this, researchers focused on the R136 cluster in the Large Magellanic Cloud, which is the most luminous star cluster in the Local Group and has a high star formation rate. By analyzing spectroscopic data from MUSE, researchers were able to identify 113 B-type stars in R136 and 20 of these stars were found to be Be-type stars. Be-type stars in R136 were found to have rotation rates that were significantly faster than those of B-type stars, which suggests that rapid rotation may be the key to differentiating between B-type and Be-type stars. Additionally, researchers found that the fastest rotating stars were the least luminous, which is consistent with the concept of conservation of angular momentum.

The inverse text standardization problem seeks to identify the underlying text
representation from a given, potentially noisy dataset. While this problem has
long been a challenge in natural language processing, recent advances have made it
more accessible. However, successful solutions still heavily rely on dataset quality.

This paper demonstrates a Faber-Krahn type inequality for the first eigenvalue of 
the Hermite operator when subject to Robin edge conditions, and investigates 
the essential spectral singularities that arise.

Deep Kernel Gaussian Processes utilize a tangent kernel to approximate complex processes. However, most tangent kernels assume non-exchangeable properties, which limits their application in cases involving multiple output variables and dependency in time. We introduce the tangent kernel as "non-exchangeable" and explore its potential in modeling relationships, especially in cases with multiple output variables. We then propose a new non-exchangeable tangent kernel that accounts for interdependencies between data points and is flexible enough to model relationships between data points. We also present a non-exchangeable tangent kernel that is based on a variational autoencoder and is capable of modeling relationships between data points. We evaluate the effectiveness of these kernels using multiple metrics and find that they are able to accurately model relationships, especially in cases with multiple output variables and interdependent data points.

In one-dimensional systems with non-Hermitian elements, the exceptional point topological characteristics can be altered when subjected to a correlated environment. When a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian is placed in a peer-coupled arrangement with its Hermitian counterpart, the topological exceptional points are eliminated due to the loss of Kramers' pairing, resulting in the merging of degenerate states. This phenomenon is exemplified in a model consisting of Dirac fermions coupled to a parity-breaking impurity and paired with their parity-preserving counterparts, where the model exhibits no topological properties around the real axis due to the absence of exceptional points.

Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of synthesizing spoken speech. However, the goal of generating natural-sounding speech as produced by human speakers remains unachieved. Research has shown that characteristics such as warmth, energy, and formality in speech can be identified and characterized through speech patterns. We have developed a system capable of automatically extracting these traits from spoken speech, incorporating them into synthesized speech, and verifying the authenticity of the synthesized speech for each individual. We have successfully integrated these traits into the Watson text-to-speech system, and listener evaluations revealed significant differentiation between synthetic speech produced by individuals and a baseline control group.

A variant of the Standard Model featuring a gauged $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry, along with a modular $A_4$ symmetry, is proposed to account for luminous dark matter. Within this model, the $\bar{\theta}$ term is eliminated, and a dark matter candidate arises from the model in the form of a neutral right-handed Majorana lepton that interacts solely with the $Z_{R}$ boson. As a result, the model predicts a dark matter mass of approximately $O(100)$ GeV and a dark matter density of $O(10\%)$ of the total dark matter content. Furthermore, the model yields a condition for the modular $A_4$ symmetry that corresponds to the "residual" symmetry known as $\Delta T_{\rm mod} = \text{diag}(1, 1, 1, 1)$. Consequently, the model offers a means to generate small masses for charged leptons in a manner consistent with observations, and it demonstrates that neutrino masses can arise via the seesaw mechanism even when the modulus has a real fixed point at $s=1$. As an example, the model illustrates mass generation for three neutrinos, with the corresponding $\theta_{13}$ mixing angle falling within the range of experimental observations.

Investigating low-energy dynamics within triaxial nuclei involves analyzing the Gyrating Band (GB) approximation method introduced in this research. The method combines the Proximity Centroid Separation (PCS) technique with the Wigner-Eckart theorem. The Gyrating Band approximation is based on a new concept called "minimal length" derived from the generalized uncertainty principle. This concept yields a confinement potential with a triaxial shape, prompting an investigation into its characteristic Gyrating Bands across a nuclear energy spectrum. Utilizing the PCS technique combined with the Wigner-Eckart method, the Gyrating Band approximation is demonstrated to effectively describe configurations and energies associated with Gyrating Bands. A computer code, named GYRABAND, has been developed to generate GB configurations and energies for selected nuclei. The GYRABAND code is available for download at the specified hyperlink.

Golay complementary sets are a type of orthogonal class with unique properties that generalize phase shift keying (PSK) or continuous phase modulation (CPM) to multiple carriers, allowing for direct modulation and multi-carrier transmission. They can also be applied to carrierless modulation and other techniques. The authors present a novel method for producing complete sets of Golay complements for any number of phases, capable of handling even phase counts that are not multiples of four. The new technique is based on a different approach to class orthogonalization, using a convex optimization method to a conventional Hadamard-based approach. The results show that it is possible to produce Golay complements for any number of phases, including those that are not multiples of four. The paper also presents a method for determining frequency shifts that can be used to determine the exact frequency locations of Golay complements. The authors demonstrate the potential of these complements for real-world applications by showing their spectrum and discussing their use in cognitive radio and other techniques.

Changes in a scene's material or spatial arrangement can result in local alteration events appearing as distinct spectral or spatial patterns. For instance, a break in a branch or changing land use/trade activities can be identified as a shift in spectral patterns in a landscape. Small occlusions or changes in lighting conditions can also cause alteration events, especially when analyzing a scene over multiple periods. Detecting these alteration events in a continuous surveillance of a scene is essential for various applications such as tracking objects moving into an area or monitoring environmental changes. A scene classification module may identify unusual patterns in a scene but often fails to pinpoint the exact location of alteration events. A more effective approach involves using a deep convolutional autoencoder to recognize alteration events without requiring ground truth data. However, this method can be hindered by the lack of a separate training set and by the feature space's dimensionality. A novel deep feature combination alteration detection method has been developed to address these issues by combining the features of different autoencoders to improve the representation of alteration events in a shared feature space. This method uses a soft voting mechanism to identify the most likely location of alteration events. Our results show that this method performs better than other approaches, producing fewer false alarms while still detecting genuine alteration events.

We analyze the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in real molecular fluids and their corresponding model interactions. Our study focuses on three-body effects, enabling accurate predictions of both properties simultaneously. By adjusting the model to closely replicate the corresponding fluid's pair and three-body characteristics, we can generate models that closely match experimentally measured property trends. To achieve this, we employed an entropy extrapolation method to determine an optimal model, which closely replicates the fluid's observed entropy profile. Subsequently, we calculated the viscosity of this optimized model using ab initio molecular dynamics, resulting in a very good match for the observed viscosity. This approach demonstrates the potential for developing highly accurate models that effectively capture the complex interplay between molecular fluid properties.

We've developed a cyclical cosmology model, combining the Lambda CDM model with a cyclical model of the universe. This results in a more complex equation for the Hubble parameter, H, taking into account both the Lambda CDM phase and the cyclical model's contribution. Using the LC CDM cyclical model, we analyze two models: the first is identical to the Lambda CDM model, with a deceleration parameter q_1 equal to 0.55, and the second is a cyclical model with a deceleration parameter q_2 fluctuating between 0.55 and -1 as the universe transitions between its Lambda CDM and cyclical phases. By assuming that the Lambda CDM and cyclical phases occur uniformly, we estimate the total number of e-folds for each phase. This investigation employs two methods to estimate the deceleration parameter q_2, utilizing the properties of the LC CDM cyclical model to understand its behavior and its potential implications for observations such as BICEP2, Keck Array, and Planck.

The invariant-set hypothesis is a superdeterministic approach to addressing the cosmological constant problem. In this study, we explore this concept within a hidden-variable framework based on a modified de Broglie-Dirac theory. Here, the vacuum state is described as consisting of a network of interacting, long-range gravitational fields generated by de Broglie-ghost particles. Specifically, we examine the case where our inert matter particles correspond to de Sitter space environments characterized by positive cosmological constant values, while de Broglie-ghost particles correspond to anti-de Sitter space environments characterized by negative cosmological constant values. In this context, our invariant-set hypothesis proposes that the total gravitational potential energy associated with the network of interacting de Broglie-ghost particles is zero. In this study, we explore the implications of this proposal for its ability to explain the observed value of the cosmological constant by demonstrating that it is not possible to achieve a zero-total-energy state through a symmetric arrangement of de Broglie-ghost particles. In particular, we demonstrate that any network of interacting de Broglie-ghost particles, subject to gravitational constraints, cannot be zero-total-energy due to a fundamental energy imbalance arising from the long-range interactions between the de Broglie-ghost particles.

Keyphrase extraction is an essential task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), 
whereby a document's main topics are identified and condensed into significant 
words or phrases, facilitating quicker and more in-depth reading. Foragers 
of factual knowledge on the internet could greatly benefit from this technique, 
not only enhancing their comprehension but also saving time by reducing their 
information search. Unfortunately, the current NLP models are not designed 
to run efficiently on low-powered devices, hindering their use on devices such 
as smart speakers, head-mounted displays, and other wearable technology, which 
limits their application to practical tasks like real-time summarization or 
search results.

To address this challenge, we experimented with a lightweight sequence 
classification model, evaluating its effectiveness in comparison to other 
techniques. Our findings suggest that this approach is viable, and we propose 
a simple yet efficient method for extracting keyphrases from documents, 
thereby enabling more compact and readable document representations that can 
be easily searched on devices with limited resources.

We examine the dimer representation of the Ising spin-1/2 model on a two-dimensional lattice and also apply it to two flavors of Majorana fermions in a 2D space with a non-zero boundary, coupled with a gauge field. In the case of the Ising model, we focus on the dimer representation at its free boundary conditions. In the scenario involving fermions, each Majorana fermion has a free and confined dimer representation. We then determine the energy spectrum of these systems on an arbitrary 2D lattice and derive a set of dimer rules for them. We also derive the Ward identities for dimer configurations and show that these are equivalent to the Ward identities for the original models. We also calculate the critical dimer energy in the large and small limit of the lattice spacing. We also show that the dimer energy is conserved under a duality transformation. We also calculate the dimer energy in the lattice duality transformed Yang-Mills theory. We also calculate the lattice gauge coupling from this. We also calculate the lattice gauge coupling from the dimer energy in the lattice duality transformed Yang-Mills theory. We also show that the lattice gauge coupling approaches a constant as the lattice spacing approaches either a large or a small value. We also show that the lattice gauge coupling approaches a constant as the lattice spacing approaches either a large or a small value. We also calculate the lattice gauge coupling from the dimer energy in the lattice duality transformed Yang

In the field of machine learning and data analysis, the group-Lasso has emerged as a crucial regression technique that encourages regression coefficients to be zero outside predetermined groups. However, in scenarios involving categorical data, traditional group-Lasso is impeded by the need to first convert data into a continuous format or perform expensive preprocessing steps to create continuous features. In contrast, the enhanced group-Lasso method leverages the power of modern sparse statistical techniques to efficiently handle high-dimensional categorical data in both its boosted and original formulations. By adopting these advanced techniques, the enhanced group-Lasso is capable of producing consistent results in the absence of knowledge of group boundaries, thus providing a highly versatile and efficient technique for tackling complex regression problems.

In recent years, the development of hypervisors has garnered significant interest, with most research focusing on hardware virtualization technology. The feasibility of using hypervisors in embedded real-time systems has also been explored, with existing solutions revealing limitations when it comes to multi-threaded user programs. The primary challenges posed by existing solutions include potential program delays, priority inversions, and dependencies on hardware drivers. To address these limitations, a new design for hypervisors in embedded real-time systems is needed. A hypervisor called T-Visor was developed for multi-core processors with hardware virtualization technology, designed to manage mixed-importance user programs efficiently. The T-Visor design achieves real-time guarantees by leveraging preemption, roll-back, and isolation capabilities, with user programs benefiting from these mechanisms without additional overhead. The performance of T-Visor was evaluated using a benchmark test platform, with results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in embedded real-time systems.

When working with massive datasets like panoramic images, accurate image stitching is crucial to achieve a wide field of view. We introduce an approach utilizing an inertial gravitational frame of reference to establish correspondence between images. The intrinsic image representation, inspired by the concept of gravitational potential, provides a globally consistent coordinate system. We demonstrate that this representation yields a well-defined metric and curvature. The curvature serves as a feature for stitching, providing a global perspective. The accuracy of our approach is validated through experiments on real-world datasets.

Our research explores the complex network dynamics, specifically in chimeras, 
wherein two distinct entities with identical parameters are coupled with each 
other and also with a shared, fully connected system. This setup ensures that 
all entities are interconnected. Initially, we induce randomness within these 
entities, and then allow their dynamics to unfold over time. This randomness 
disperses as the chimeras evolve, and we examine how this distribution 
affects the overall behavior of the system. This investigation enhances our 
understanding of how heterogeneity impacts synchrony and stability in complex 
networks.

Contemporary controller learning methods typically concentrate on developing efficient solutions with optimal energy usage, but often overlook the uncertainty of system parameters and model errors, which can result in controllers that are highly susceptible to failures when applied in real-world scenarios. This paper proposes a novel approach called Resilient Controller Learning (RCL) to produce controllers that can adapt and perform effectively even when there are discrepancies in system models or unexpected faults with a significant impact on system dynamics. A probabilistic model is established to represent parameter uncertainty and model inaccuracies, and the resilient controller is defined as the optimal decision-making strategy to achieve the highest average performance under probabilistic system conditions. A novel policy search algorithm is developed to efficiently identify the resilient controller, and the proposed method is successfully applied to a complex system and compared against conventional approaches, demonstrating its superiority in terms of robustness and adaptability in the face of system disruptions.

Building on multi-layer diagrams from diagrammatic Hecke algebras, we introduce novel algebras called higher slice rings. As a consequence, we derive the ring structures of higher slice quotients from endomorphism algebras of multi-layer diagrams. Moreover, we present the isomorphisms between the symmetric endomorphism algebras of multi-layer diagrams and the higher slice quotients, yielding new categorifications of group algebras. Additionally, we prove that the endomorphism algebras of multi-layer diagrams have global dimension two, which is the first example of its kind in diagrammatic categories.

We explore the relationship between single-party entropy and multi-party entropy in chaotic tensor networks, specifically focusing on the mutual information between a part of the network and its entire initial state. Our findings demonstrate that this mutual information, known as the refracted entropy, grows at a rate proportional to the entropy of the initial state, both in terms of entropy and entanglement width, but only after a initial transient period. This conclusion is drawn from the analytical derivation of the asymptotic growth rate of the refracted entropy. As a result, we speculate that this relationship could serve as an indicator of chaos in more complex systems.

Living systems rely on information from their past experiences to make decisions and form decisions that can be passed on to future generations. In contrast, physical systems do not retain information about their past behavior. In this study, we explore under what conditions heritable information can persist in a system with random fluctuations, even when the system itself changes over time. Our findings reveal that for information to be maintained, it must be tied to changes in the system in a specific way and must be transmitted consistently from one state to another. We demonstrate these concepts using simple models of how heritable information might influence a system's changes, such as mutations in evolution.

A smooth generalization of the three-dimensional H\'{e}non map is defined by the iteration formula $x_i=(x_{i-1}+a-\frac{\alpha x_{i-1}^2}{2},y_i=(y_{i-1}+b-\beta x_{i-1}y_{i-1}).$ In this paper, we focus on the pullback phase space of the generalized H\'{e}non map for specific values of the parameters $a$ and $\beta.$ The pullback phase space represents a two-dimensional space consisting of all fixed points $(x,y)$ corresponding to a given map $(x,y)\mapsto (x+a-\frac{\alpha x^2}{2},y+b-\beta x y).$ We have obtained detailed visualizations of the pullback phase space for various values of the parameters $a$ and $\beta.$

The Ashtekar variables, primarily used in loop quantum gravity research, offer a clear representation of the quantum gravitational state space. Employing these variables results in the formulation of a super-Poincaré algebra, which, when used to define generators of translations, reveals the presence of a fundamental "discrete gravity" momentum, influenced solely by the holonomy. Further investigation into its structure shows that this momentum is based on a simplified version of the Riemannian gravitational path integral. Consequently, it has been proven that the momentum space is made up of sets of geodesically connected states, which can be either conformally equivalent or orthogonally separate. Additionally, it has been found that the discrete gravity momentum's Stone-von Neumann uniqueness theorem applies only to spaces with SU(2) or SO(3) symmetry. Which of these symmetries is present in the momentum space depends on whether the corresponding space's geodesic structure exhibits a conformal or orthogonal nature.

In a specific setting of Catalan numbers for the reduced hyperoctahedral group $[m,s]$, we focus on the distributions of hook lengths that are multipled by two or three. We derive an explicit formula for $\mu_{2,m,s}$ and $\mu_{3,m,s}$, representing the number of such distributions in terms of $m$, $s$, and $\pi$, where $\pi$ is a partition of $m$. We express $\mu_{2,m,s}$ and $\mu_{3,m,s}$ as products involving $B$-quosients, where $B$ represents a specific integer divided by another. We show that $\mu_{2,m,s}$ and $\mu_{3,m,s}$ can be expressed as products of $\mu_{2,m',s'}$ and $\mu_{3,m',s'}$ for suitable $m',s'$, related to $\pi$, which enables us to easily compute $\mu_{2,m,s}$ and $\mu_{3,m,s}$ for small $m$ and $s$. We utilize this result to count the number of reduced, semiregular Brauer diagrams with specific labels on vertices and multiplicity $s$, particularly finding that $\mu_{2,9,1}=1048576$ and $\mu_{3,7,1}=5760$.

We analyze the tunneling process of a particle through a potential barrier influenced by a clock's magnetic field, leading to a particle's partial transmission. This particle tunneling phenomenon is linked to a clock's Larmor precession, causing a shift in energy levels that affects a clock's timing accuracy. We investigate how particle spin interactions impact this timing accuracy, specifically for particle-barrier systems with aligned and misaligned external magnetic fields.

Our research focuses on calculating the leading twist distributions for P-wave mesons, utilizing both relativistic QCD distribution amplitudes and nonrelativistic hard-collinear effective theory (HET). We found that the leading distributions for P-wave mesons involve the twist 4 contributions, specifically d_4(u) and d_4(a0) in the scalar and pseudoscalar channels. These twist 4 contributions dominate at a twist 2 subtraction point and are influenced by a single parameter. In contrast, the twist 2 and twist 4 distributions for pseudoscalar mesons have distinct subtraction points and are scale-independent. Additionally, the leading distributions for P-wave vector mesons have twist 2 and twist 4 contributions, while those with axial vector properties exhibit additional twist 3 contributions. However, the twist 3 contributions can be shown to be subleading and are therefore negligible.

Researchers have proposed a range of quantum devices that can be described as switches, allowing a quantum signal to be redirected through various paths. Currently, most studies on quantum switches have been based on theories involving finite number of qubits or superconducting circuits, which often rely on linear models. A novel approach has been taken to develop an exact model of a nonlinear quantum switch by utilizing a Bose-Einstein condensate, which is inherently nonlinear. This model can be used to control quantum signals, regardless of their linear or nonlinear nature, and can be represented as a non-symmetric tridiagonal matrix. An analytical method has been developed to solve the eigenvalue problem associated with this matrix, revealing distinct properties between linear and nonlinear scenarios. Moreover, the study's findings have been experimentally verified and could potentially lead to the creation of more complex, multi-output devices.

Our analysis extends the soft factorization theory to any order of soft terms, building on the double-soft theorem from string theory and scattering amplitudes. This expansion leads to factors of infrared divergences at any given order in perturbation theory, prompting an expansion of the BMS algebra to include higher-order spin terms. Key outcomes of our research include predictions about higher-order infrared divergences, the form of higher-order amplitudes in gravity, and the properties of higher-order radiation in gravity, including its polarization and behavior at long wavelengths. These predictions apply to any massless gravity theory, including general relativity, gravity theories with massive fields, and higher-dimensional gravity theories.

We introduce NOEL, a novel neural structure capable of learning in real-time and
integrating new data into existing models continuously. Unlike traditional
approaches, NOEL can adapt without pre-requisites such as predefined model
architectures, separate training and testing sets, or data balancing. By
merging online stacking ensembles with online learning, NOEL continuously trains
and combines models as data arrives. Since NOEL models are continuously updated
and rewritten during the learning process, analysis and visualization tools
like TensorFlow Hubble Suite become ineffective. To overcome this, our approach
employs sample-based representations and a graph neural network to provide
insights into NOEL's inner workings. We test NOEL's capabilities on real-world
80s video games and find that it outperforms well-known deep learning models,
including ResNet, VGGNet, and SqueezeNet, when using fewer resources.

In generalized shapes theory, which is a modification of the classical one, a new theorem has been proven for four-dimensional Riemannian metrics. This change yields enhanced geometric and algebraic outcomes. A key consequence of this enhancement is that the underlying metric can have an arbitrary signature, not just the standard + - signs.

Permutation functions and complete permutation functions over a non-commutative ring have distinct, unique characteristics. In this research, specifically focusing on q-adic fields of the form $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3n}}$ with q not equal to 0, we examine permutation functions and complete permutation functions relative to the subfield $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Our study reveals that a permutation function, relative to a subfield, is equivalent to a complete permutation function if and only if it has no 'zero' component when evaluated using the basis of the extended field $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Utilizing this finding as a stepping stone, we have developed necessary and sufficient criteria for a permutation function, relative to a subfield, to be representable as a complete permutation function, specifically in the context of q-adic fields of the form $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$.

A major public health concern in many low-income countries is intestinal worm infections, caused by large intestinal parasites that prompt severe health issues and stifle personal and national development.  To address this issue, we must first accurately diagnose the worms, a process typically done visually by healthcare workers, but can be challenging.  We used Deep Belief Networks to train a computer-based system to identify and categorize intestinal worms using microscope image data, comparing it to a convolutional neural network model.  Our results indicate that the DBN model offers a viable alternative for computer-based diagnosis and can be combined with other techniques, like those employing smartphones for data collection, to create a comprehensive package for intestinal worm diagnosis.

This paper presents a dual approach for estimating a family of non-zero-sum linear 
investment and reinsurance models that take into account a Markov-modulated jump process. 
To achieve this, two distinct methods are employed: a maximum likelihood approach and a 
Bayesian method utilizing Markov Chain Monte Carlo techniques. Both approaches demonstrate 
high convergence and accuracy for various scenarios, with convergence speeds being heavily 
influenced by the Monte Carlo error. Numerical experiments show the effectiveness of the 
estimation methods in a variety of situations and reveal that the Bayesian approach offers 
greater precision on average.

For highly maneuverable aircraft like the F-16, generating steady flight from a takeoff or landing configuration can be challenging due to initial control angle constraints. To address this issue, a new method using the stochastic dual simplex algorithm to find suitable control angles is presented, along with a genetic filter to eliminate infeasible solutions. This approach is demonstrated in the PIDA flight of the F-16 on NASA's VFS simulator, where a flight trajectory is planned using linear matrix inequalities and the control angles are optimized under actuator saturation constraints. The genetic filter ensures the feasibility of the control angles, and the stochastic dual simplex algorithm efficiently identifies feasible solutions, ultimately resulting in steady flight.

The fundamental low-energy interactions between pions and nucleons are a fundamental aspect of strong interactions, yet this sector remains theoretically underdeveloped due to a lack of data and challenging experimental conditions.  Chiral effective field theory provides a framework to describe this complex interactions, but its application relies heavily on unknown high-energy form factors, which can be determined by incorporating higher-order calculations.  We examine the high-energy behavior of several form factors within the context of the relativistic chiral effective theory.  We discovered that the radial and transverse response functions at high energies are essentially the same and can be described by a single form factor.  We calculated the high-energy behavior of several Pion-Nucleon form factors and found that loop corrections have a minor impact on the electromagnetic multipole moments, with the exception of the D1(3) and E2(3) moments.  We also observed that the loop corrections fail to account for the empirical D1(3) moment, while the E2(3) moment matches the experimental value.  We conclude that the empirical properties of low-energy pion-nucleon interactions cannot be adequately explained by one-scale form factor descriptions and suggest the presence of a resonance, specifically the rho, to account for the observed moments.

The Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) experiment is one of the primary detectors for the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), where it is responsible for analyzing the particle interactions created by the collision of protons that occur at energies up to 13 TeV. The LHC is situated at CERN in Geneva, Switzerland, and consists of a circular 27-mile tunnel containing proton beams that circulate around it. The CMS is an essential part of the LHC's four major detectors, and it utilizes a superconducting solenoid to produce a magnetic field that is able to detect the particle trajectories.
