This review delves into the application of high-dimensional dynamic network methods in the analysis of temporal influence graphs, specifically focusing on the estimation and evaluation of influential nodes. By comparing static and dynamic influence models, we highlight the advantages of dynamic approaches in the identification of varying influential behaviors throughout time. Furthermore, this review discusses the utilization of dynamic influence models in the determination of temporal causal relationships. Ultimately, this research area is expected to continue expanding with advancements in machine learning and the increasing availability of temporal big data.

The concept of stable set balance was proposed in reference \cite{Bal}, offering a potential tool for modeling task scheduling with resource constraints via CNF constraints. This led to the question of whether the balanced stable set problem is NP-hard, prompting an investigation into its computational complexity. Before addressing the main question, we first demonstrate that the scenario with two stable sets is in P and resolves unbalanced scheduling problems easily. However, for the general case, we show that the problem is indeed NP-hard by reducing it from the 3-partition problem. This reduction reveals a key insight: for any given instance of the balanced stable set problem, if it has a solution, we can use this solution to solve an instance of the 3-partition problem. This reduction holds even when the initial instance of the balanced stable set problem is restricted to two stable sets. This finding implies that the balanced stable set problem is at least NP-hard, with an approximation resistance implication.

In recent years, digital forensics has gained significant interest, and the concept of reversible concealment has emerged as a crucial aspect. The main goal of reversible concealment is to hide secret information within a digital carrier without compromising its original usability. Moreover, it's essential to verify the authenticity of the concealed data and extract the original information without leaving behind any trace. This study focuses on an advanced method of reversible concealment using a Bayesian Neural Network (BNN). The proposed BNN method utilizes a BNN to encrypt and another BNN to decrypt the secret information, ensuring that only the BNN can extract the data. The study also demonstrates the feasibility of the proposed method by conducting experiments and evaluating its effectiveness.

By utilizing complex magnetic configurations and varying rotation rates, we simulate the development of magnetic fields in stars and planets using the mean-field framework and a kinematic dynamo method. Our study focuses on turbulent influences, applying both empirical and theoretical formulas to determine magnetic field evolution. We discovered that neglecting certain turbulent effects results in an overestimation of magnetic field growth, which may lead to an incorrect understanding of how these effects limit dynamo activity. Furthermore, accounting for all turbulent influences yields a wide range of possible dynamo solutions, underscoring the need for realistic magnetic field observations and theoretical constraints to accurately model astrophysical dynamos.

Our observations of the star-forming galaxy NGC4945, made using the ALMA at 12cm, 23GHz, and 110GHz frequencies, reveal a large (70kpc) molecular outflow. The 110GHz spectrum shows an almost circular shape, almost coincident with the host galaxy's edge, while the 23GHz and 12cm data show a smaller (20pc) region highly compressed and heated. Our data support a two-phase outflow model, with cold and hot components originating from the 110GHz and 23GHz/12cm frequencies, respectively. The outflow's kinetic energy is approximately 2% of the galaxy's star formation energy. The 110GHz data also show evidence of star formation rates and molecular gas depletion times. The 23GHz and 12cm data, on the hand, show lower star formation rates. The outflow may be driven by the star formation energy, but the outflow may be regulated by the galaxy's disk thickness and the interplay with the surrounding intercloud medium. The outflow may also be influenced by the presence of an active galactic nucleus. The outflow may be the source of heavy elements seen in the outflow, but the interplay with the galactic wind may be the ultimate source of the elements. A version of the quasilinear diffusion equation that accounts for magnetic field alignment is used to model particle and energy transport in magnetized plasmas. This equation incorporates a Fokker-Planck description of particle and energy resonance interactions with turbulence. It is based on a combination of kinetic and thermodynamic principles and fundamental plasma stability and quasilinearity assumptions. This paper presents a novel numerical approach to solving the equation, which is an extension of existing conservative numerical methods for linear diffusion equations. A semi-Lagrangian scheme is developed to handle the nonlocal diffusion term, maintaining both conservation properties and a high degree of accuracy, which is essential for simulating transport phenomena in quasilinear diffusion equations accurately.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative IMPLICIT METhods were developed for solving standard continuous-time systems directly, without the need for discretization. In this work, the relevant theory and formulas from the original paper were updated to incorporate variable stepsize capabilities. Specifically, the implementation of Newton's method was modified to support variable stepsize methods. In addition, the error control implementation was also revised to allow for adaptive time stepping. Consequently, the resulting code achieved first-order convergence in both space and time. As a practical application, the variable stepsize implementation was combined with the previously developed sparse algorithms. When applied to sparse systems, the new implementation resulted in a significant reduction in computational cost, achieving orders of magnitude improvement while maintaining sparsity. Moreover, the adaptive implementation of error control yielded optimal results, with no additional errors introduced due to over- or under-meshing. As a result, the computational cost was further reduced.

This note addresses the issue of exponential robust stability in Banach spaces for c0-semigroups. Specifically, it focuses on the robust stability of c0-semigroups with asymptotic stability, demonstrating that for a family of semigroups {T(a), a>0} generated by A(a), if there exists a bounded, positive, and symmetric operator B such that A(a) + B^2 is uniformly resolvent-compact, and the inclusion Im(BA(a)) is contained within the positive spectrum of T(a) for all sufficiently large a, ensuring that the spectral bound of T(a) does not exceed zero, implies the exponential robust stability of the family of semigroups {T(a), a>0}. This condition simplifies to the Lyapunov inequality 0 >=<BA(a), x> for all x in the Banach space, and the fact that the set {<Bx, x>: x in the Banach space} is bounded, and the proof illustrates that this characterization is sharp. Moreover, the discussion shows that the condition of uniform resolvent-compactness is necessary, and the example demonstrates that the exponential robust stability does not necessarily imply the uniform resolvent-compactness of the family of operators A(a).

MuMuPy is a software for simulating interactions between dimuonium (a bound state of two muons) and ordinary matter, allowing users to model specific systems and output wave functions in Gaussian basis. Version 2.0 of MuMuPy includes support for modeling atoms and ions containing dimuonium, as well as the ability to calculate electromagnetic interactions and perform non-relativistic propagation in external fields. MuMuPy can be used in two ways: as a standalone Python program or as a combined C++/Python library. MuMuPy comes with a graphical user interface, referred to as the MuMuPy Factory, which enables users to input necessary information and execute calculations. MuMuPy's code is publicly available under a permissive open-source license, and it is suitable for use in research across multiple fields, including quantum chemistry and materials physics.

Portfolio managers assess success by comparing themselves to peers or market standards, not just by overall wealth, but also by relative performance. Total wealth indicates a portfolio's absolute prosperity, while relative wealth measures its relative success. Both notions of success encompass total wealth as a subset, making them essential aspects of a portfolio manager's mindset. This study examines a portfolio manager's optimal portfolio choice when utility is derived from both total and relative wealth through a power function, revealing that the optimal portfolio continuously adjusts between the market portfolio and full market equivalence as the utility parameter varies, and that the optimal portfolio parameters exhibit distinct patterns as the utility parameter increases.

Using simulations of galaxy evolution, it is discovered that the least massive galaxies are the first to have their gas content ejected, which then forms the earliest intergalactic medium. This IGM of these low-mass galaxies has unique properties such as lower metal content and hydrogen ionization. However, further analysis shows that the metal content of this IGM is overestimated due to the impact of stellar feedback. Correcting for this effect, it is found that the metal content of this IGM is in line with the expected outflow velocity at the time of ejection. This suggests that feedback from supernovae plays a key role in removing gas from low-mass galaxies, which in turn contributes to the early IGM. Early IGM of these galaxies is also enriched by feedback from active galactic nuclei, which is in line with observations of the metal content in these galaxies. When a Fermi liquid becomes coupled to another system that doesn't behave as a liquid, it can cause a phase transition known as a pseudogap. We found that there's a way this pseudogap can occur without affecting the behavior of the original Fermi liquid. This happens when there's a local interaction between the two different types of particles, and it causes a gap to form in the less stable state while the Fermi liquid remains unchanged. We studied this phenomenon using two different models, and found that it's possible for gaps to form in both models in a way that doesn't destroy the behavior of the Fermi liquid. This could be an explanation for strange behavior seen in certain superconducting cuprates, and it also gives us a way to study the different parts of a system that becomes coupled in a failure of Fermi liquid behavior known as an unconventional normal state.

This paper investigates the divergence properties of finite Thompson groups, specifically their generalized versions, and the braided Thompson groups. It shows that in finite Thompson groups, T, T0, T2, and T2,3, n is greater than or equal to 4, implies a nontrivial element a has a divergence n-3, and for m being 1 or 2, a similar nontrivial element b in Mr has a divergence m-1. It's also found that in finite Thompson groups, T, T0, and T2,3, a nontrivial element a has a divergence n-2, and for m being 1 or 2, a similar nontrivial element b in the braided Thompson group Br has a divergence m-2. Further, it's demonstrated that finite Thompson groups, T, T0, and T2,3, are perfectly closed with respect to divergence.

This paper explores the application of the Complete RAG framework in the context of question answering tasks. Specifically, it involves using both the denotation retrieval component and the generative aspect to create answers. Unlike previous work, this research delves into generating answers without relying on pre-existing denotations. Additionally, this framework is applied to a question answering task in a manner that contrasts with existing approaches. Important nuances in the implementation are identified and assessed, and the effectiveness of this approach is evaluated on the HOTPASS dataset. Notably, this paper also examines the potential risks and limitations of this framework.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a logarithmic weight given by $\log \frac{1 + a(x)}{1 + a(\frac{1}{x})}$, where $a(x)$ is a given polynomial of degree $n$. Our analysis also covers the asymptotic behavior of the zero locations, Nikiforov-Savitch weights, and the degree of the best approximation by polynomials in the interval $[-1,1]$ for functions in the class of continuous functions on $[-1,1]$ with a logarithmic weight. Our findings are verified by examining specific examples.

Creating an effective automated summarization system necessitates a substantial pool of high-quality human annotators, but locating qualified annotators proves to be a significant challenge. In this study, we examine our efforts to recruit experienced annotators for MTurk tasks related to natural language understanding, such as summarization. We analyze our recruitment strategy, including the use of job title and description optimization, as well as professional sourcing via Turkers with demonstrated expertise in linguistics and natural language processing. Additionally, we explore the potential of using qualification frameworks to identify and retain skilled annotators. Our findings suggest that job description optimization is the most efficient method for attracting qualified workers, and that using job titles alone is insufficient. Furthermore, we discovered that using qualification frameworks to filter annotators before a task begins can help us identify and retain reliable workers.

Text-video retrieval has gained significant interest in recent times, with a variety of applications in social media platforms. The task of matching text and video inputs necessitates a model that can simultaneously analyze both modalities. The existing state-of-the-art approaches for text-video retrieval typically employ two-stream transformers that process text and visual streams separately, merging them through multi-head attention to facilitate cross-modal interaction. However, we observe that the visual stream does not need to be concerned with understanding lengthy text inputs, and conversely, the text stream does not need to capture complex visual information. Based on these observations, we introduce the TS2-Net, which incorporates token shift and choice modules to process text and visual streams independently while enabling cross-modal interaction. The TS2-Net outperforms previous approaches and sets a new benchmark, achieving a remarkable 83.9% mAP on the MSRVTT-M dataset.

We explore a theoretical model that expands the neutral current sector of the flavor-changing top quark interactions. This model can be justified within the framework of a complete and consistent theory, such as a vector-like lepton model, where a new neutral current influences lepton flavor violation processes without affecting their overall strength. The model's implications on lepton flavor violation processes, particularly in the $K$ and $\tau$ systems, are examined to establish model constraints based on existing limits. The model also predicts the occurrence of specific, rare top quark processes, such as the $ct$ and $ct'$ mixing-induced flavor-changing neutral currents, which can be tested at the Large Hadron Collider.

In the realm of network science, the development of new methods to create realistic, studyable network models has been a pressing need. To address this, we've introduced a novel approach consisting of a hybrid random network generation strategy, specifically designed to capture the nuances of real-world networks' characteristics. Our method combines two mechanisms: preferential attachment, which focuses on connecting nodes to those with existing connections, and uniform attachment, which involves connecting new nodes to the network in a more random and uniform manner. By balancing these two processes, we've developed a scalable, simple, easy-to-parametrize method that effectively replicates the characteristics of large real-world networks, including small-world properties, specific degree distributions, and separation between nodes with high and low degrees.

This research introduces a real-time method for identifying the source and frequency of radio frequency interference affecting wireless devices. By analyzing data from various locations, it's possible to categorize interferences from unknown patterns. A Convolutional Neural Network model was developed and trained on 1,536 single-point recordings and 4,608 multi-point recordings from 10 unique sources. To evaluate performance and accuracy, CNNS were applied to 1,536 single-point recordings and 4,608 multi-point recordings. Results indicate high classification accuracy for single-point and multi-point recordings, exceeding 90%, demonstrating the effectiveness of CNNS in detecting RFI and accurately classifying multiple signals.

In a gravitational field generated by a cosmic string, the behavior of particles described by the Klein-Gordon equation is studied. A novel approach is employed to analyze interactions between particles and the gravitational field, focusing on the relationships between vorticity, energy, and charge. It is discovered that, without a gravitational field, there are no interactions between these physical properties. However, when particles are affected by the cosmic string spacetime and an additional space-like displacement is introduced, new interactions become apparent. Specifically, connections between energy and vorticity as well as between energy and charge emerge.

A nonatomic, locally compact Hausdorff space algebra of measures on a compact Hausdorff space possesses the uniform continuity property when every continuous algebraic transformation yields a uniformly continuous sequence, given the original space is not too finely divided. This condition is equivalent to the existence of a locally compact, unique measure that is invariant under this transformation and, when such a measure exists, it must be the only one and this criterion defines a new class of spaces, distinct from those that are locally compact but not finely divided. Furthermore, space $\mathbb{Q}^{\mathfrak{p}}$ where $\mathfrak{p}$ is a prime number exhibits the above property and, in fact, it serves as an example of a space that is finely divided and also, in this context, it is shown that the associated algebra of measures possesses the uniform continuity property despite not having a continuous compact topology.

This article presents a novel observable, known as the Recoil Proton Alignment (RPA), which emerges when measuring the Deep Inelastic Scattering cross-section off a nuclear target over a wide range of momentum transfers. Calculations indicate that the RPA remains relatively unaffected by the complexities of the bound state, unlike many other non-perturbative effects. Moreover, the RPA is sensitive to the distribution of Generalized Parton Distribution Functions within the proton, much like the longitudinal proton form factor. Notably, the RPA's magnitude is expected to be substantial, on the order of 10 to the negative 4, making it a promising observable for the Hall A and Jefferson Lab's CLAS12 experiments to measure and utilize.

Artificial intelligence systems have become ubiquitous in our daily lives, yet the term 'intelligence' remains a subject of debate and variation in context. To address this, this paper will examine the core principles of artificial intelligence and propose a classification system to organize the diverse applications and definitions within the field. Building on this framework, the paper will then explore the concept of superintelligence, with a specific focus on a subcategory known as hybrid intelligence, which combines human and machine intelligence in collaborative modes of operation. Key aspects of hybrid intelligence will be examined, including its potential forms and benefits, as well as the challenges and obstacles that need to be overcome to realize its potential. Ultimately, the paper will examine the current state of hybrid intelligence within the broader field of artificial intelligence, with a specific emphasis on its future enhancements and applications.

Our research involves exploring the behavior of a quantum fluid that is influenced by strong correlations and spin-orbit coupling. Specifically, we utilize the density-matrix renormalization group method to study a strongly correlated bosonic system on a two-dimensional lattice near the quantum critical point in the presence of spin-orbit coupling. This system exhibits unique characteristics such as a non-traditional phase that is marked by spatial patterns of spin and orbital ordering and a superfluid phase with a modulated structure. Utilizing the results of our calculations, we investigate how the specific energy levels in the system change in response to temperature at its lowest energy state and discover a phenomenon in which higher energy levels become more sensitive to temperature at the quantum critical point. Furthermore, we investigate how the shifting energy levels impact the collective excitations in the system.

Consider a finite abelian group $G$ of order $r$, and let's construct a graph degeneration sequence for it. This graph, called the Levi graph $L(G)$, has vertices representing the group's elements and incident edges corresponding to the group's operations. A subset of vertices in $L(G)$ is independent if the group operations involving its elements do not result in the identity element. We're interested in how the size of these independent subsets changes as the operations in $G$ are eliminated in a specific order. This investigation leads to the definition of a family of $r$-partite graphs called $(r-1)$-degradable, and it is shown that these graphs coincide with the Levi graphs of finite abelian groups.

We delve into the AdS/CFT duality by exploring a two-dimensional AdS space in quantum gravity, where we encounter substantial type IIA solutions that expand in the spatial direction. These substantial solutions allow for straightforward calculations in AdS/CFT, resulting in the capacity for both regular and irregular bulk-boundary correlators. Notably, our findings include the presence of conformal symmetry breaking, infrared divergence, and the capability for finite energy states to transition into the vacuum. Additionally, we observe the presence of ghosts and non-causal behavior in the theory, where information paradoxically travels faster than the speed of light in specific scenarios. These peculiarities are resolved through the application of a mirror principle, revealing the substantial theory to be equivalent to a theory on an S-shaped AdS space. By demonstrating this equivalence, we show that the substantial theory can be mapped to a theory with a conformally invariant Wilson line, thereby allowing us to compute bulk-boundary correlators for these S-shaped AdS spaces.

We introduce a kernel based kernel-learning method for determining the covariance function of a given data set. A thorough mathematical examination of common Gaussian Process (GP) kernel types reveals that most of these operators can be broken down into two fundamental components - a l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l l

The forthcoming muon colliders will likely operate muons as clusters to enhance luminosity, but this may be compromised by in-flight decay muon beams generating in-plane background noise. In this scenario, optimizing transverse beam shapes and profiles can help minimize interference with collider measurements. Here, various beam manipulation techniques, including tailored distributions, tailored trajectories, tailored time structures, and tailored spatial separations, are examined for their potential to counteract the nuisance signals. Using muon collider design assumptions, a simulation demonstrated the feasibility of reducing the effects of in-flight decay muon beams by introducing tailored trajectories, and further research is being conducted to refine this method.

Neural networks' ability to process and learn from sparse data is crucial for numerous applications, including signal processing and communication systems. However, traditional methods introducing sparsity into deep neural networks through differential penalties are not compatible with standard gradient-based optimizers. We propose a new approach, differentiable sparsification, which leverages a regularized conveyance property to make sparse data suitable for neural networks. This innovative method not only reduces computation and memory requirements but also infuses sparsity into deep networks. We demonstrate that our differentiable sparsification technique can be easily integrated into existing data flows and applied to various neural network layers. Moreover, our approach can be utilized for not only data sparsity but also parameter sparsity, including structural sparsity. We successfully implement differentiable sparsification in a neural channel to enhance signal quality and find optimal solutions that are infeasible with conventional sparse methods.

According to the principles of quantum mechanics and statistical physics, gases of bosons, such as those with two spin states, should not be prevented from transforming into a uniform, spin-polarized state when exposed to an external magnetic field, as this configuration minimizes energy levels. However, our research reveals the presence of a fundamental, inherent barrier to this transition that originates from the collective behavior of bosons under low-level magnetic fields in a specific dimension. This barrier is triggered when the magnetic field interacts weakly with the bosons and is strong enough to cause a change in spin alignment. Instead of reaching a uniform state, the system becomes trapped in a non-uniform, spin-fluctuating state that retains a specific quantized value of spin, contradicting conventional understanding. This discovery may lead to the development of materials with long-lasting, non-uniform quantum properties and could be experimentally verified in systems of ultracold atoms or bosonic fermion mixtures.

Past research has identified "test odor" as a prevalent issue affecting developers' productivity during bug fixing and maintenance tasks. However, little is known about developers' perceptions and concerns regarding test odor. To fill this knowledge gap, our study conducted a survey among active Java developers, asking them to describe instances of test odor in their projects and its impact. The results show that approximately 10% of developers reported test odor in their projects, with a third of these instances affecting multiple developers. Interestingly, our findings suggest that test odor is not always viewed as a critical issue, with some developers considering it a minor problem. Based on our analysis, potential solutions to address test odor include improving communication among developers and implementing smell detection tools.

This research explores a novel approach to solving nonconvex hybrid optimal control problems, building upon the differential inclusion concept. By incorporating the Filippov principle, we establish a corresponding minimum problem for cost functions optimized through the sweeping procedure. Our method employs measurable control functions to accommodate nonconvex constraints, thereby extending traditional convex cases. In addition, we provide a comprehensive example demonstrating the efficacy of this innovative strategy.

We introduce an enhanced version of the KKMCee event generator, which creates initial events for simulated data in future lepton collider experiments. In contrast to traditional generators that generate final-state photons and leptons separately, KKMCee incorporates both weak and electromagnetic interactions in its algorithm, enabling accurate predictions for final-state lepton and photon pair productions simultaneously. Leveraging the established accuracy of the KKMC generator for standard model processes, KKMCee has incorporated new physics capabilities such as heavy flavor production via heavy gauge boson decay and the production of heavy leptons, along with their subsequent decays. Additionally, KKMCee includes its Electroweak Correction (EWCON) module for both weak and electromagnetic interactions. In this research, we detail the implementation and validation of KKMCee for its three-legged and four-lepton final states and evaluate its performance and precision in various benchmark cases.

Heart rate variability (HRV) is a critical indicator that offers insights into cardiac health and resilience. Inter-beat intervals (IBI), a key component of HRV, can be accurately measured using electrocardiography. We propose a novel deep learning strategy, based on a Time-Auxiliary Recurrent-Insulated-SuR (TARIS) model, for IBI duration estimation from ECG signals. This approach uniquely employs a dual configuration for its hidden layers, allowing for optimal performance and reduced errors. We have tested and validated the TARIS model on the public INCART2 dataset, and the results demonstrate its superiority over existing time-distributed models.

The application of tensors is rapidly expanding across multiple disciplines, and research in these areas heavily relies on processing, analyzing, and manipulating complex multilinear data. The tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) plays a crucial role in data reduction, and its most effective method is the higher-order (high-order) SVD, which offers significant performance advantages. However, the high-order SVD faces significant scalability issues, and alternative approaches like matrix-based methods and greedy algorithms have been proposed, although they have limitations. In response to these challenges, this study presents a new stochastic algorithm for t-SVD, which offers a guaranteed solution with a specified level of accuracy and can be adapted to accommodate an optional specified level of passes through the data. The proposed algorithm also has a time complexity variant that is not dependent on matrix size, and it is suitable for use on systems with limited resources, and it can be further improved by incorporating parallel processing capabilities using libraries like OpenMP.

Networks and organization charts are excellent examples of graphs that change over time with the addition and removal of nodes and edges. To effectively process these types of dynamic graphs, embeddings that stay consistent when updates are applied have been developed. However, the field of graph embedding is still new, and there is a lack of research on how to maintain consistency in evolving graphs where nodes and edges change over time. Specifically, we are studying how to update graph embeddings when nodes merge, split, or form new connections. Our method for evolving graph embedding involves creating separate embeddings for nodes and edges, and then combining them in a way that reflects their relationships. By using these embeddings, we are able to design systems for processing evolving graphs and demonstrate their effectiveness using real-world data sets. Our results show that our method is more accurate than existing methods, and we are able to respond to changes in these types of graphs in just a few steps.

A novel method is introduced to describe deuterium and hydrogen isotopes with no intrinsic angular momentum, utilizing a $^3$H ground state and four neutrons as building blocks. By combining the $^3$H ground state with the $-4$ quantum numbers of the neutrons in the one-body space, the rotational constants for deuterium and hydrogen isotopes with no intrinsic angular momentum can be calculated. Additionally, this method allows for a straightforward inclusion of interactions between the particles, facilitating the calculation of energy corrections. Using this method, the binding energy of the $^7$H ground state is calculated to be 0.036 MeV, in line with the most recent experimental findings of binding energy as 0.118 MeV.

A previous finding by Nirenberg in 1981 revealed that for values greater than or equal to 5, the Poincaré mapping does not have a zero point in the given range. Our investigation focuses on whether this result persists for lower values of k, with a particular emphasis on k equal to 3 and 4. To achieve this, we aim to solve a k+2 variational problem on the upper half of the k+1 dimensional sphere. To demonstrate that the Poincaré mapping does not have a zero point for k equal to 3 and 4, we must show that the mountain pass level in these cases is greater than 1. Our approach to achieving this involves blow up arguments on the (k+1) dimensional sphere S^4 for k equal to 3 and 5, and on S^7 for k equal to 4, which yields a positive solution to the problem.

Current self-supervised learning approaches for deep representations rely heavily on correlations between similar and dissimilar data, often using contrastive or auto-encoding techniques. These methods use simplified measures of data similarity, such as Euclidean distance, which may not accurately reflect the complexities of real-world data. In our study, we use the Sinkhorn distance as a more robust tool for measuring data similarity in deep representations. This parametric distance is well-suited for deep self-supervised learning, as it can be easily linearly combined with network outputs. We propose a novel self-supervised method, based on the Sinkhorn distance, which surpasses state-of-the-art results on image and point cloud datasets. Notably, our approach performs well even with a simplified linear backend.

In various settings, local contact tracing efforts have been instrumental in identifying COVID-19 cases and curtailing disease spread. Although a national contact tracing system was established in the UK, local initiatives continued to flourish, particularly in Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. This study aimed to evaluate the impact of these local efforts in England by examining the relationship between their performance and the reduction in infections. Utilizing data on local tracing collaborations' case findings and test numbers, a comparative analysis was conducted to assess the non-linear correlation between these metrics and declining hospitalizations and infections in England. The results revealed a strong association between local collaboration performance and decreases in hospitalizations and infections. Notably, a 10% increase in local case findings was linked to a 1.1% decrease in hospital admissions and a 0.8% decrease in infections, indicating a beneficial effect of these local efforts. These findings have significant implications for public health policy, suggesting that supporting local tracing collaborations can enhance national contact tracing efforts and inform policy decisions.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is essential for understanding their characteristics and evolutionary patterns. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey, we conducted a study of the Melotte 72 open cluster, which is located at a distance of approximately 2,800 parseks from the Earth. Our analysis focused on calculating the cluster's physical parameters, including radial velocity, distance, and global photometry, through a multi-step process. We first created a proper motion diagram by filtering Gaia DR2 data to an 8 parsek radius around Melotte 72, and confirmed its membership using color-magnitude and Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams. Our subsequent analysis revealed a mean distance of 2,800 parseks with a 20 percent margin of error, radial velocity of 111.21 kilometers per second, and determined the cluster's physical parameters, including age (460 million years), mass (1.43 times 10 to the power of 3) solar mass), and initial mass (2.15 times 10 to the power of 3) solar mass), and confirmed the Gaia DR2 distance through infrared and radio observations. Our findings also showed that Melotte 72 is rotating at 0.623 angular velocity, which is consistent with the parameters of young open clusters.

We are examining the topological characteristics of Gaussian trajectories in low-dimensional spaces, specifically in the form of 2D polygonal trajectories given a sequence of directional changes. These changes are treated as independent, normally distributed random variables with a mean and variance. When the trajectories become increasingly sparse, meaning the sample mean of these directional changes decreases, we are investigating how the Betti numbers behave under this condition. These topological measurements indicate the number of holes or obstacles in the trajectory's space, and our results show that one Betti number behaves differently in the sparse regime. Specifically, the first Betti number exhibits a change from polynomial to exponential likelihood as the sample mean decreases and the variance remains constant. Conversely, the other Betti numbers retain characteristics of high-dimensional trajectories in the sparse regime. These findings are then extended to estimating topological features of n-step Gaussian processes, and our predictions demonstrate improved accuracy in the sparse regime. These advancements are attributed to reduced dimensionality, and our estimates outperform Monte Carlo simulations in this context.

We propose an eye-in-hand camera adjustment method that can be learned from just one image. This method is suitable for tasks on robotic workbenches and requires minimal setup. It works by defining 3D object features based on inverse robot kinematics and then using them to calculate pose adjustments that maximize a perceived object edge map. To achieve this, we first develop an edge detection algorithm that can handle varying camera poses. Next, we transform raw image edges into 3D format using pose-conditional deep networks. Finally, we frame the camera adjustment problem as a non-rigid registration issue and devise a straightforward optimization method to solve it. Experimental results show that our technique consistently yields accurate results on a variety of robotic platforms.

In conventional reinforcement learning, the focus is on using rewards to create policies that achieve a desired outcome under an expert's guidance. However, this approach has limitations because experts may not always be available or the provided rewards might be incomplete. A novel method called reverse reinforcement learning (RRL) has been developed to create a reward function that aligns with an existing policy considered optimal. By inverting this process, RRL overcomes the challenges associated with traditional reinforcement learning. However, existing RRL methods are restricted to using unsupervised strategies for finding the optimal policy and might not work well when faced with complex tasks. This restriction could result in RRL-generated reward functions that are unsuitable for guiding the agent toward the optimal policy. To address this limitation, we have introduced a constrained reinforcement learning (CRL) framework that allows the agent to discover policies that meet specific constraints, and it can be used in conjunction with RRL to produce the desired reward function. By leveraging the strengths of both RRL and CRL, our proposed approach has been demonstrated to successfully learn the optimal policy under various task scenarios, and it even enables the discovery of policies that violate expert-provided hints in a partially observable laboratory setting.

The European Space Agency's GAIA mission, a core objective of which is to create a detailed 3D chart of the galaxy's numerous bright celestial bodies, is poised to significantly advance our understanding of the galaxy's structure. This report outlines the mission, its performance, and the initial scientific findings from the first data releases. Additionally, we explore the ongoing processing and expected future science outputs, as well as newly emerging opportunities for future space astronomy missions to build upon the galaxy's mapping mission legacy.

Vertex decomposers and order decomposers are key to computing tree decompositions, a crucial concept in treewidth. While vertex decomposers can be identified efficiently, order decomposers are computationally infeasible. A notable challenge arose from Bodlaender's algorithm, which requires converting any tree decomposition into an equivalent order decomposition within a set time bound, but this limit is approaching a constant multiple of the well-known time bound for treewidth computation. To address this issue, researchers proposed vertex partition schemes to speed up order decomposition construction. A new scheme, compact vertex partition, is introduced here to improve upon existing methods. When applied to vertex decomposers, this scheme yields order decompositions with a reduced number of constituents compared to previously proposed schemes. By combining this scheme with vertex decomposition algorithms, it can be shown that tree decompositions can be computed within a time bound comparable to treewidth computation, a significant improvement over previous efforts. When combined with order decomposers, this scheme enables the creation of order decompositions within a time bound of $n^{O(\log (kn)/\log n)}$, a result applicable to $n$-vertex graphs with treewidth $k$. This result is a crucial step in Bodlaender's algorithm, and when combined with known algorithms, it implies that tree decompositions can be computed within a time bound of $2^{n-1}$.

Network analysis is a widely used method with applications across multiple disciplines. This method has been employed with varying types of network data, including different assignment and interpretation methods. To provide a unified framework for analyzing networks, we define specific interpretations and identify necessary prerequisites. Specifically, we focus on directed networks where edge weights represent the strength or capacity of connections, and examine local grouping processes in this context. This examination leads to three primary interpretations of weighted directed connections: structural, operational, and effective. Key local measures for a node in a weighted directed network include its neighbors, proximity, and centrality. To establish a consistent analysis approach, we define specific requirements for choosing neighbors in this context, including the necessity of a limited degree and presence of the strengthening principle. This principle states that a node's local connections should be more strongly connected to the node itself than to other nodes.

Researchers have recently introduced Physics-informed Neural Networks (PINNs) which combine the power of deep learning with physical principles to solve complex problems quickly and with high accuracy. However, due to their reliance on physical principles, there is potential for authorized machine learning where only certain parameters can be adjusted, similar to how experiments are conducted. To achieve this, we develop a method to estimate the error rate in PINNs. By testing this method, we find it is possible to obtain accurate approximations of a solution with a specified level of precision and express this in the form of a hypercube. Using our error estimation method, we are able to derive constraints for the allowed training region of PINNs and identify the minimal number of parameters needed for a given level of precision.

Epidemiological research utilizes statistical methods to analyze the patterns and causes of diseases, which often employs spatial analysis techniques to measure and evaluate disease trends over time. By integrating machine learning and geostatistics, researchers can uncover insights into the underlying factors driving disease development. To illustrate the value of this combined approach, this study focuses on examining the impact of atmospheric pollution on the incidence of chronic respiratory diseases in children. By leveraging geostatistical methods and the machine learning techniques of Random Forest and k-means clustering, researchers can identify key atmospheric contaminants and areas of high risk. By merging epidemiological research with the capabilities of geostatistics and machine learning, researchers can make more comprehensive contributions to their field.

A novel technique for differentiating Majorana peaks from other peaks through tunneling spectroscopy is developed, focusing on the specific energy associated with Majorana modes. Utilizing Ohmic dissipation via resistive electrodes introduces individual Landau levels broadening into the system, resulting in a step function with defined upper and lower bounds. Majorana-related peaks are distinguished by exhibiting symmetrical upper and lower bounds, with other peaks displaying asymmetrical ones. However, in cases of very low counts or with multiple peaks, including a Majorana peak, simulation results suggest that peak identification can be challenging. Nevertheless, by adjusting the count to an optimal level, based on the width of the Majorana-related step and the overall count, it becomes possible to accurately distinguish between the two types of peaks.

To analyze linear bandits, a scenario where decisions are based on dynamic action choices based on current observations, we studied various types of action sets and their impacts on regret bounds. Our research focused on non-asymptotic regret bounds applicable to any number of time steps. We found that action sets with a finite number of elements and certain structural properties influence regret bounds significantly. These findings not only contribute to traditional linear bandit research but also have practical applications in related areas such as multi-armed bandits in the classical learning community.

Graphene with gaps can exhibit two unique properties: the orbital Hall effect and the valley Hall effect. Although they share some similarities, we found that the orbital Hall effect stems from a distinct mechanism that does not involve the same type of interference that typically leads to valley polarization in graphene with gaps. By studying a specific type of graphene with quasiperiodic corrugation, we discovered that our model shows no indication of valley polarization but does exhibit orbital Hall conductivity, confirming that the orbital Hall effect represents an independent phenomenon.

Big tech companies utilize Graph Neural Networks to make informed decisions about advertising placement, but current solutions are limited by their reliance on perfect training data, which is often compromised due to contamination during data collection. This issue is particularly pronounced in the case files, which serve as controls but can be tainted by matching real-world scenarios. We address this challenge by developing a reinforcement learning-based method that identifies and strips away contaminated data within graph datasets, which is essential for effective GNN-based ad placement decisions. We frame this issue as a multi-stage decision problem where our algorithm aims to eliminate contaminated data instances while minimizing losses, which is framed as a Reinforcement Learning problem. We implement this idea using a Value Decomposition Network, which enables parallel processing of GNNs to eliminate contamination. Our approach demonstrates superior results on public datasets and a custom ad placement dataset in comparison to baseline methods, including Graph Random Walks and Transfer Learning.

The process of matching object catalogs relies on identifying the best associations between objects of the same nature located at the same sky position, and requires accurate astrometry. Although the astrometric errors can be significant in some datasets, we've found that incorporating additional photometric data can be used as an ancillary constraint for matching objects. By developing a method that utilizes photometric data to refine the probability of matching, and prioritizes the most likely associations, we've achieved improved results on mock sky catalogs with limited astrometry errors. This approach is particularly beneficial for datasets with large astrometric errors, such as those obtained from small telescopes or crowd-sourced observations, and can be applied to a variety of object types.

In 1974, Karp established a minimum edge cover for hypergraphs, which has been used to solve problems in recursion theory and set theory. The Karp edge cover can be translated into a particular infinite hypergraph $H_\omega$ with countably infinite vertices. The validity of an assertion regarding minimal edge covers for $H_\omega$ determines whether a specific set theory question has a solution, specifically the continuum problem. The assertion states that every minimal edge cover of $H_\omega$ is a proper minimal edge cover, which has been shown to be false. The proof of this falsehood yields two separate results, which were also obtained through other lines of inquiry. The first result concerns a particular class of infinite hypergraphs, which have been shown to always possess a proper minimal edge cover. The second result is tied to a particular type of countable ordinal, which has been shown to be the least among a class of ordinals, which has been shown to be invariant under a particular operation.

In domains like medicine and materials science, extensive knowledge is often organized into large, interconnected systems called ontologies. These systems consist of interconnected entities called concepts, which are used to describe various aspects. Researchers frequently need to understand relationships within these ontologies, particularly when exploring large collections of related information. However, existing visualization tools primarily focus on hierarchical connections, neglecting other types of relationships, such as those for scientific subfields or materials composition. To address this limitation, we present OntoPlot, a novel visualization that displays non-hierarchical connections within ontologies. OntoPlot uses an interactive, circular layout to display concept relationships, which can be of any type, through innovative and interactive visualization mechanisms. OntoPlot's design enables researchers to gain insights into how concepts interconnect across hierarchical boundaries, showcasing its potential with real-world ontology examples.

This paper outlines a novel approach to semi-supervised end-to-end automatic speech recognition systems. We've developed an inter-domain penalty to leverage unpaired speech-representation and audio-waveform data, enabling our system to generalize beyond paired data during training. Additionally, we've adapted a CycleGAN-based method to move paired data from one domain to the other, improving our system's performance in cross-lingual and cross-acoustic domain settings. Our experiments, conducted on the WSJ-TIMIT dataset, demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in improving recognition accuracy when used in conjunction with existing semi-supervised systems.

Bayesian active inference offers a unified framework for robot navigation and
control.  Within this framework, navigating independently by processing
sensory data in a sequential manner reveals itself to be an unsolved difficulty.
  A novel approach is presented in this paper to tackle the challenging task
  of initiating inference without prior knowledge and achieving robustness to
  inaccurately modelled sensory processes.  By employing a Bayesian approach
  to initialise the model, and incorporating heterostatic entropy terms, an
  unsupervised method is developed to train predictive models using temporal
  predictive coherence.  A practical implementation on a mobile robot
  demonstrates that these methods successfully facilitate model training and
  efficient prediction of sensor data.  Comparison experiments using
  homostatic and heterostatic cross-entropy methods demonstrate that the
  proposed heterostatic methods exhibit greater efficiency and provide more
  accurate predictions.

The Soret effect, or thermal diffusion, describes a concentration gradient established within a mixture of fluids subjected to a temperature difference. Research has focused on the Soret effect primarily using small molecules, yet modern technologies involving soft matter can generate significant thermal diffusion. To fully leverage these applications, it's crucial to comprehend the factors influencing the Soret effect in soft matter. This work examines the contribution of internal degrees of freedom to thermal diffusion in soft matter, based on molecular dynamics simulations. To illustrate the findings, two models of flexible molecules are employed. The results show that the Soret effect is largely driven by the movement of flexible molecule segments, rather than individual atoms. Additionally, the effect of temperature and free segment distribution depend solely on the free molecule length. This discovery facilitates the development of free length free energy models to describe thermal diffusion in flexible molecules.

In music, the challenge of automated composition evaluation remains an unsolved problem, with human aesthetics and emotional resonance at its core. This study introduces a novel, two-stage approach to composition evaluation that leverages the capabilities of large-scale language models. Firstly, it identifies significant ideas in a composition and compares them to those in a high-quality reference piece. Secondly, it predicts human ratings of compositions by analyzing the aesthetic connections between ideas. We successfully demonstrated the effectiveness of our model on the Mozart K12 dataset and the C Major Piano Dataset, and found that it outperformed traditional machine learning models and human composers in terms of predicting human ratings. Notably, our model also provided valuable stylistic feedback that aligned with human preferences.

In pedestrian-based applications such as surveillance, self-driving vehicles rely heavily on estimating box annotations to understand scene context and agent behavior. However, unsupervised domain adaptation methods in this field are limited, with most relying on online inference to adapt to new environments. To address this issue, a novel approach has been developed that utilizes an off-the-shelf object detector, with a focus on eliminating false positive predictions from domain-specific object boxes. A novel ranking loss has been introduced that compares matched pairs of online and offline box detections. Additionally, a mechanism has been proposed to handle unmatched tracks from online and offline boxes. The approach demonstrates domain adaptation performance comparable to existing methods, with the added benefit of significantly reducing false positive predictions in domain-specific object box results.

This study presents a novel approach to generating high-quality audio from images, leveraging a VAE-based model that produces auditory embeddings. A conditional STTN model then refines these embeddings, aligning them with audio dynamics. A text-to-speech model is used to convert the refined embeddings into audible waves, resulting in a full audio signal. Notably, this method achieves natural sounding results even with limited input images and short sequences, without requiring ground truth audio data.

In a throwing motion, the point of release significantly impacts overall performance. We examined the impact of mistakenly changing the point of release, focusing on four key factors: arm motion, throwing speed, arm position, and visual appearance. Through a user study with 11 participants, we analyzed the effects of varying the point of release on these factors and found that points close to the final position yielded the best results. This study revealed valuable insights that can inform the development of virtual throwing tasks to enhance user experience.

This study presents an innovative NMT system that leverages n-gram-based models to guide decoding in a tree-based structure, incorporating syntax-inspired links to enhance translation accuracy and reduce search space, respectively. A novel "constituency" link, driven by a separate tree parsing model, is used to manage sentence structure, while a "coherence" link based on contextual similarity helps filter excessive and unnatural links, ultimately improving translation quality by omitting unnecessary connections. Our research demonstrates the superiority of this design over traditional NMT by over 1.0 BLEU on the NIST MT task and outperforms state-of-the-art models on the WMT 2019 tasks for Chinese-to-English NMT.

The formation of molecular clusters in interstellar clouds can significantly impact key chemical reactions and should be taken into account by astrochemists when modeling these reactions, especially in the gas phase. To facilitate accurate astrochemical modeling, it's essential to have a library of binding energies for various molecular clusters, which we have compiled in the Binding Energy Assessment Platform. This platform contains a database of quantum chemical binding energies for diverse molecular groups, which can be used to create accurate binding energy distributions. To ensure the platform is versatile, we have included different methods for describing molecular clusters, such as those based on diffusion Monte Carlo and genetic algorithm methods. To showcase the platform's utility, we have demonstrated its application to the formation of H3O+ from H2O and an H+ ion, which is a critical step in the formation of many astrophysically relevant molecules. By making the Binding Energy Assessment Platform freely available, we hope to support the development of more accurate astrochemical models.

Multiplicative stochastic processes can be categorized into three types: random walk, Wiener process, and geometric Brownian motion. The first two lack a minimum limit, leading to unbounded growth. In contrast, the geometric Brownian motion incorporates a minimum limit, albeit one that's randomly generated. To facilitate practical applications, a new type of multiplicative stochastic process has been developed, incorporating a sample-dependent minimum limit. The proposed process can be used in both theoretical and practical scenarios, such as financial analysis and risk assessment. The introduced concept can also be expanded to the higher-order stochastic process.

Quantum systems exhibiting dynamic behavior can be effectively modeled using complex mathematical transformations, known as one-forms, which facilitate the prediction of quantum phenomena. However, the expectation values of observables in these systems pose a challenge, as they require high-functioning mathematical objects, known as deep forms. To overcome this limitation, a new approach has been developed, utilizing random Clifford circuits of varying depths to model expectation assessments. The method involves using Clifford-specific cohomology and intermediate forms to reach intermediate results with depths matching intermediate sizes, offering a trade-off between depth and accuracy. The approach has been demonstrated to produce accurate outcomes across all sizes, including deep systems, applying to any quantum circuit, regardless of complexity. The method's feasibility has been demonstrated through simulations of smaller quantum systems, modeling the Ising model and the Fredkin gate.

The research focuses on the reflection and outgoing coefficients for water waves generated by a plate in the Davey-Stewartson II equations, where two solutions exhibit a significant dependence on $|k|$ behavior in the high-frequency limit. Utilizing a recent nonlinearity operator expansion method and plate wave pattern approximations, the findings show that the research contradicts previous studies on water waves generated by a localized source in deep water, where the frequency spectrum behavior was found to be $|k|^{-\frac{1}{2}}$.

Recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of ensembles, particularly Sibyl variants, in improving text categorization accuracy. This work takes this concept further by developing more robust and accurate methods for text categorization tasks. We've successfully applied variations of the Sibyl algorithm to address both noise and concept drift issues in three real-world text categorization datasets. Additionally, we've used a Baysian-based approach to determine the optimal number of submodels within each ensemble, allowing for automated submodel creation via an automated threshold selection process. Our experiments show that these ensembles consistently outperform traditional classifiers, with the top-performing ensembles achieving a significant improvement of over 40% in classification accuracy.

In the realm of supervised learning, a meta-learning approach trains models to handle multiple related tasks simultaneously. Our focus is on linear regression, where we've developed a method to identify a low-rank regression matrix that effectively solves a multitude of linear regression problems with shared data across multiple tasks. By employing an optimization technique inspired by the natural gradient, our method can achieve theoretical convergence in a few iterations, yielding a linear decrease in convergence rate. Moreover, under realistic assumptions regarding task data alignment, our approach guarantees that the regression matrix accurately replicates the ground truth up to an error margin proportional to the square root of the number of samples. Notably, this method can be executed without any prior knowledge of the number of tasks, and it even outperforms competing baselines in real-world datasets.

Research into lightweight neural machine translation models for low-resource conditions has gained interest, with quantization and model pruning being prominent methods to decrease computational costs. Another technique, neural architecture selection, is used to identify more stable components within the original model and eliminate less essential parts. This study compares the stability of quantization and neural architecture selection when applied to a small translation model. Experiments on the Turki NLP datasets showed that neural architecture selection resulted in better performance, with an average improvement of 0.66 and 1.15 BLEU points respectively, using one and two neural architecture selection iterations. In contrast, quantization yielded an average improvement of 0.23 and 0.38 BLEU points in one and two iterations respectively. Additionally, the results indicate that neural architecture selection offers more control over which parts of the model are affected, as compared to quantization.
